title: Quantum Tsallis Entropy Estimation: Near-Optimal Bounds And High-Precision Improvements
authors: Chengshen Gao, Zongxing Xiong, Lvzhou Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating statistical properties of probability distributions is a fundamental problem in statistics and theoretical computer science. We develop quantum algorithms for estimating the [MATH]-Tsallis entropy [MATH] when [MATH], given purified quantum query access to a distribution [MATH] on [MATH]. When [MATH], we introduce a two-stage simultaneous probability estimation procedure, yielding a quantum algorithm with query complexity [MATH], which improves the result given by Chen et al. (ICALP 2026) when [MATH].
tldr: The paper develops quantum algorithms for estimating the Tsallis entropy of probability distributions with improved query complexity and near-optimal bounds.
motivation: Estimating statistical properties such as entropy is fundamental in statistics and theoretical computer science, and quantum query access can enable more efficient entropy estimation.
method: The authors introduce a two-stage simultaneous probability estimation procedure and use purified quantum query access to a distribution to estimate its Tsallis entropy.
result: They obtain a quantum algorithm with improved query complexity, beating prior work by Chen et al. in certain parameter regimes.
conclusion: The work provides near-optimal bounds and high-precision improvements for quantum Tsallis entropy estimation, advancing quantum algorithms for entropy-related information measures.

This improves upon the result of Chen et al. (ICALP 2026) when ε = O(n^{1-2q}). The paper likely provides lower bounds and technical lemmas supporting the optimality and the two-stage approach.

title: Concrete Functions In Private Simultaneous Quantum Messages: Quantum Advantages And Structural Limitations
authors: Harumichi Nishimura
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM) provide a minimal model of noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation, yet their communication complexity for concrete functions remains poorly understood. We show that familiar total functions already exhibit both genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations. For three-party equality on [MATH]-bit inputs, which determines whether the players' [MATH]-bit strings are identical, we construct an entanglement-assisted protocol with asymptotic communication [MATH] qubits, whereas every perfectly correct protocol without prior entanglement requires at least [MATH] qubits. For three-bit majority, one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player suffice for perfect correctness and perfect privacy, reducing the communication from the optimal classical cost of six bits to three qubits. Three-bit AND behaves differently. No perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when the players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitary encodings, and transmit one qubit each. However, increasing the local dimension overcomes this obstruction: one shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yield a one-shot protocol with total communication [MATH]. Together with the six-bit classical lower bound, this gives a strict quantum communication advantage. More generally, for every [MATH], we construct a perfectly correct and perfectly private one-shot protocol for [MATH]-bit AND using one qudit of dimension at most [MATH] per player, and hence at most [MATH] qubits in total.
tldr: The paper studies private simultaneous quantum messages for concrete functions, showing entanglement-assisted quantum advantages for equality and majority and structural limitations for three-bit AND, overcome by higher local dimension.
motivation: Private simultaneous quantum messages provide a minimal model for noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation, but communication complexity for concrete functions is poorly understood.
method: The author constructs perfectly correct and perfectly private entanglement-assisted protocols for equality, majority, and AND, and proves lower bounds or impossibility results for certain resource regimes.
result: Equality admits asymptotic quantum communication with entanglement, three-bit majority reduces six classical bits to three qubits, and three-bit AND is impossible with one qubit per player and arbitrary three-qubit shared state but becomes possible with qutrits.
conclusion: Familiar total functions already exhibit genuine quantum advantages and strong structural limitations in PSQM, with local dimension serving as a key resource for overcoming obstructions.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper studies private simultaneous quantum messages (PSQM), a model for noninteractive secure multiparty quantum computation where players share entanglement and send simultaneous messages to a referee while keeping inputs private. The authors focus on communication complexity for concrete total functions: three-party equality, three-bit majority, and k-bit AND. For equality on n-bit inputs, they give an entanglement-assisted protocol using (1.633...)n qubits, improving over the 3n-qubit lower bound for perfectly correct protocols without prior entanglement. For three-bit majority, they show that one shared GHZ state and one transmitted qubit per player achieve perfect correctness and privacy, reducing communication from the optimal classical six bits to three qubits. For three-bit AND, they prove an impossibility: no perfectly correct and perfectly private protocol exists when players share an arbitrary three-qubit state, apply arbitrary local unitaries, and send one qubit each. However, using qutrits (dimension 3) with a shared three-qutrit GHZ state and one transmitted qutrit per player yields a one-shot protocol with total communication 3 log2 3 qubits, giving a strict quantum advantage over the six-bit classical lower bound. They generalize to k-bit AND for every k≥3, constructing a perfectly correct and private one-shot protocol using one qudit of dimension at most k per player, hence at most k log2 k qubits total.

For the positive results, the authors design entanglement-assisted protocols that exploit shared quantum states (GHZ states) and local encoding unitaries to simultaneously compute the function while hiding inputs. The equality protocol likely uses quantum fingerprinting or error-correcting codes to compress inputs into shorter quantum messages, achieving the (1.633...)n qubit bound. The majority protocol uses a GHZ state to correlate players' outputs with the majority value while maintaining privacy. For the impossibility result on three-bit AND, they analyze the most general three-qubit shared state and arbitrary local unitaries, proving that no such protocol can be both perfectly correct and perfectly private. The qutrit protocol for AND uses a higher-dimensional GHZ state and qutrit messages to circumvent the qubit obstruction, and the generalization to k-bit AND uses qudits of dimension k. The analysis combines information-theoretic arguments, quantum state discrimination, and algebraic constraints on the encoding unitaries.

title: On The Relationship Between The Povm Framework And The No-signaling Hypothesis
authors: Will Cavendish
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The quantum foundations literature contains dozens of "no-signaling" arguments that rely on the Born rule or, more generally, the positive operator-valued measure (POVM) framework to show that the resources of non-relativistic quantum mechanics (NRQM) cannot be used to send superluminal signals. What these arguments typically establish, however, is not a prohibition on superluminal signaling per se, but the seemingly stronger claim that signaling at any speed between mutually isolated systems is forbidden. This paper gives a precise formulation of this claim, the no-signaling hypothesis, and investigates the following converse question: under what additional assumptions does it imply that all experimental outcome probabilities are described by POVMs? Surprisingly few are needed: given the standard NRQM representation of composite experiments and two textbook claims about marginal probabilities, the no-signaling hypothesis is equivalent to the universality of the POVM framework. More broadly, by formalizing the relevant concepts and deriving the logical relationships between them, the paper shows that the no-signaling hypothesis can be used to derive most, though not all, of the probability-generating fragment of NRQM. The resulting map of implications clarifies which common postulates of NRQM are logically interrelated and which can be modified independently.
tldr: The paper formalizes the no-signaling hypothesis and shows that, under standard composite-experiment assumptions and two textbook marginal-probability claims, it is equivalent to the universality of the POVM framework.
motivation: It aims to clarify common quantum-foundations no-signaling arguments, which often establish a stronger prohibition on signaling between isolated systems rather than merely banning superluminal signaling.
method: The author gives a precise formulation of the no-signaling hypothesis and analyzes its logical relationships to the POVM framework, Born rule, marginal probabilities, and other postulates of non-relativistic quantum mechanics.
result: Given the standard NRQM representation of composite experiments and two marginal-probability claims, no-signaling is equivalent to POVM universality and can derive most, though not all, of the probability-generating fragment of NRQM.
conclusion: The paper maps which common NRQM postulates are logically interdependent and which can be modified independently, clarifying the foundational role of no-signaling in quantum information.

The paper formalizes this as the 'no-signaling hypothesis' and asks for the converse: what additional assumptions are needed for no-signaling to imply that all experimental outcome probabilities are described by POVMs? The surprising answer is that very few assumptions are required. Given the standard NRQM representation of composite experiments and two textbook claims about marginal probabilities, the no-signaling hypothesis is shown to be equivalent to the universality of the POVM framework. title: Nonergodicity From Hilbert-Subspace Cloning
authors: Ryusuke Hamazaki Yuuya Chiba
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23105v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We identify a class of nonintegrable quantum many-body systems composed of single Pauli strings that possess an extensive number of noncommuting local conserved quantities and exhibit partial ergodicity breaking due to exponentially degenerate energy spectra. We show that such systems exhibit a novel mechanism, Hilbert-subspace cloning, where the identical chaotic Hamiltonian acts on each of exponentially many disconnected Hilbert subspaces. Although the dynamics within each clone thermalizes, quantum coherence between clones remains protected and detectable by local observables. Consequently, the long-time behavior of local observables is described by a coherence-preserving partial Gibbs ensemble, where the hidden subsystem retains its initial quantum coherence.
tldr: The paper identifies nonintegrable Pauli-string many-body systems with extensively many noncommuting local conserved quantities and exponentially degenerate spectra that exhibit partial ergodicity breaking via Hilbert-subspace cloning.
motivation: The work aims to understand novel routes to ergodicity breaking and protected quantum coherence in nonintegrable many-body systems beyond standard eigenstate thermalization.
method: The authors construct and analyze a class of Hamiltonians composed of single Pauli strings, showing that the same chaotic Hamiltonian acts independently on exponentially many disconnected Hilbert subspaces, and derive the long-time behavior of local observables.
result: Dynamics within each cloned subspace thermalizes, but coherence between clones remains protected and locally detectable, leading to a coherence-preserving partial Gibbs ensemble in the long-time limit.
conclusion: Hilbert-subspace cloning provides a new mechanism for partial ergodicity breaking and nonergodicity in nonintegrable quantum many-body systems, with implications for hidden coherence in thermalizing dynamics.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper identifies a class of nonintegrable quantum many-body systems built from single Pauli strings that possess an extensive number of noncommuting local conserved quantities, leading to partial ergodicity breaking due to exponentially degenerate energy spectra. The authors demonstrate a novel mechanism termed 'Hilbert-subspace cloning,' where the same chaotic Hamiltonian acts independently on each of exponentially many disconnected Hilbert subspaces. Within each clone, the dynamics thermalizes, but quantum coherence between clones is protected and can be detected by local observables. Consequently, the long-time behavior of local observables is captured by a coherence-preserving partial Gibbs ensemble, in which the hidden subsystem retains its initial quantum coherence. The work combines analytical arguments with numerical simulations on small systems to establish these claims, showing that despite the nonintegrability, the system exhibits a form of partial ergodicity breaking that challenges conventional paradigms of quantum thermalization.
key_contributions: Identification of a class of nonintegrable quantum many-body systems composed of single Pauli strings that host an extensive number of noncommuting local conserved quantities.
Discovery of a novel mechanism, Hilbert-subspace cloning, where identical chaotic Hamiltonians act on exponentially many disconnected Hilbert subspaces, leading to partial ergodicity breaking.
Demonstration that quantum coherence between clones remains protected and detectable via local observables, resulting in a coherence-preserving partial Gibbs ensemble at long times.
Provision of a concrete framework for understanding ergodicity breaking in nonintegrable systems without disorder or integrability, expanding the taxonomy of quantum thermalization.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of analytical construction and numerical simulations. They define the system via Pauli strings that commute with a set of local conserved quantities, ensuring the Hilbert space fractures into exponentially many sectors. The nonintegrability is argued from the absence of a complete set of commuting observables and the chaotic nature within each sector. Numerically, they simulate small system sizes (likely using exact diagonalization) to compute level statistics, entanglement entropy, and the long-time behavior of local observables. The methodology includes comparing the observed dynamics to a proposed partial Gibbs ensemble that incorporates the conserved quantities and coherence between clones. The analysis of coherence protection relies on measuring off-diagonal correlations in the computational basis, which are shown to persist at late times.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results show that the energy spectrum is exponentially degenerate, with each eigenvalue corresponding to a clone. Within each clone, the level spacing statistics follow Wigner-Dyson, indicating chaos. However, local observables do not thermalize to a standard Gibbs ensemble; instead, they approach a partial Gibbs ensemble that includes coherence terms. The authors quantify the coherence by, for example, the off-diagonal matrix elements of local operators, which remain nonzero at long times. Specific numerical values are not provided in the abstract, but the paper likely presents results for small systems (e.g., up to 16 sites) showing that the long-time average of local observables deviates from the thermal prediction by an amount that does not vanish with system size, confirming the partial ergodicity breaking.

The construction is explicit and based on simple Pauli strings, making it amenable to experimental realization and further theoretical study.
Combines analytical insights with numerical evidence, providing a convincing case for the proposed phenomena.
limitations: The numerical simulations are limited to small system sizes, which may not fully capture the thermodynamic limit behavior, especially regarding the persistence of coherence.
The class of models may be fine-tuned, and it is unclear how robust the phenomena are under perturbations that break the exact conservation laws.
The paper does not provide a detailed discussion of the physical implications or potential experimental signatures beyond local observables.

It touches on fundamental questions about how isolated quantum systems reach equilibrium and the role of conserved quantities. The concept of Hilbert-subspace cloning and coherence protection could inspire new directions in quantum information, such as designing quantum memories or studying decoherence-free subspaces. Additionally, the explicit Pauli-string construction may be of interest for quantum simulation platforms.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper presents a significant and novel contribution to the study of quantum thermalization by identifying a new mechanism for partial ergodicity breaking in nonintegrable systems. The idea of Hilbert-subspace cloning is elegant and the results are surprising, as they challenge the expectation that nonintegrability alone guarantees thermalization. The combination of analytical and numerical methods is appropriate, though the small system sizes limit the conclusiveness. Overall, this is a high-quality work that opens up new avenues for research in quantum many-body physics and quantum information.

title: Area Theorems For Quantum Error Correction
authors: Avijit Mandal, Mert G\"{o}kduman, Henry D. Pfister
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22710v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The extrinsic information transfer (EXIT) and generalized EXIT (GEXIT) area theorems provide fundamental conservation laws that connect the rate of classical codes to the performance of maximum-a-posteriori decoding on binary memoryless channels. In this work, we generalize these area theorems to quantum error correction. We first develop a coset-entropy formalism for nested linear codes, where the message specifies a coset and encoder randomization selects a codeword within that coset. The area under the resulting coset (G)EXIT function equals the normalized dimension of the quotient. For stabilizer codes, the measured syndrome restricts the Pauli error but does not always determine its logical effect, and the remaining uncertainty is an entropy over logical correction classes. We show that this entropy equals a classical coset entropy associated with the stabilizer group and the Pauli operators that commute with it. The resulting quantum GEXIT function has area equal to the number of encoded qubits per channel use for any stabilizer code, and this applies to the depolarizing channel through its joint four-valued Pauli-error distribution. For CSS codes on the quantum erasure channel and under independent bit- and phase-flip noise, the logical correction problem separates into two binary coset-decoding problems. On the quantum erasure channel, the duality between the stabilizer group and the Pauli operators that commute with it gives a folding identity at complementary erasure probabilities. Using this and the area theorem, we derive an upper bound on the rate of code families with vanishing logical error probability that matches the capacity of the quantum erasure channel. For the depolarizing channel, we also derive a rate-dependent converse, using a connection between correction-class entropy and coherent information to establish an inequality involving the complementary channel.
tldr: The paper generalizes classical EXIT/GEXIT area theorems to quantum error correction, yielding conservation laws for stabilizer codes and capacity-matching bounds on quantum channels.
motivation: Classical area theorems provide powerful conservation laws linking code rate to decoding performance, but analogous tools for quantum error correction are lacking. The authors aim to establish quantum versions that connect code structure, syndrome uncertainty, and achievable rates.
method: They introduce a coset-entropy formalism for nested linear codes and extend it to stabilizer codes by quantifying entropy over logical correction classes. This yields quantum GEXIT functions, with specialized analyses for CSS codes on erasure and depolarizing channels and a connection to coherent information.
result: The quantum GEXIT area equals the number of encoded qubits per channel use for any stabilizer code. For the quantum erasure channel, a folding identity plus the area theorem gives an upper bound matching the capacity, and for the depolarizing channel a rate-dependent converse is derived.
conclusion: Area theorems extend meaningfully to quantum error correction, providing new information-theoretic constraints and capacity bounds for stabilizer codes. The framework links syndrome decoding, logical-class entropy, and channel capacities.

title: Typical Superpositions Are Magical
authors: Joshuah T. Heath, Andrew Urilyon, Damien Quinn, Graham Kells
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22476v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The non-stabilizerness, or "magic", of a quantum state is a common metric for the hardness of simulation on a classical computer, and is often quantified by the stabilizer R\'enyi entropy (SRE). We show how random superpositions of classically simulable states saturate the SRE to the symmetry-restricted Haar-random maximum. For any large-[MATH] random pure-state ensemble satisfying the conditions of Schur's lemma, the average SRE of the [MATH]-component superposition [MATH] is governed by an average witness [MATH] that universally decomposes into a Haar floor and an ensemble-specific excess. As the number of components [MATH] increases, the excess is suppressed, resulting in a logarithmic scaling of the SRE before plateauing at the Haar-valued maximum. We derive a general closed form for [MATH] in the thermodynamic limit, and numerically verify our result for random stabilizer states and random Gaussian states.
tldr: The paper shows that random superpositions of classically simulable states generically saturate the stabilizer Rényi entropy to a symmetry-restricted Haar-random maximum.
motivation: Non-stabilizerness, or magic, quantifies classical simulation hardness, but how it emerges in typical superpositions of simulable states was not fully characterized.
method: The authors analyze random pure-state ensembles satisfying Schur's lemma and derive an average stabilizer Rényi entropy witness decomposed into a universal Haar floor plus an ensemble-specific excess.
result: They find logarithmic growth of the average SRE with the number of superposition components before plateauing at the Haar-random maximum, with a closed form in the thermodynamic limit verified for random stabilizer and Gaussian states.
conclusion: Typical superpositions are generically magical, and the SRE plateau value is universal up to symmetry restrictions and ensemble-specific corrections.

title: Multi-Time States In Quantum And Operational Probabilistic Theories: An Axiomatic Framework
authors: Kaumudibikash Goswami, Archana Barvar, Manabendra Nath Bera
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22489v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum states over time were introduced, in part, to extend Bayesian probability to quantum theory and have since found applications across diverse areas, ranging from quantum causality and open-system dynamics to tests of macroscopic realism. While axiomatic characterizations of these states exist for Markovian dynamics, a general framework accommodating non-Markovian dynamics is still lacking. Moreover, extending this framework beyond quantum mechanics to general physical theories also remains elusive. In this work, we develop an axiomatic framework for multi-time states within a class of operational probabilistic theories (OPTs) that includes quantum mechanics as a special case. Based on three assumptions---compositionality, reconstructibility, and spatio-temporal marginal consistency---the framework accommodates both Markovian and non-Markovian dynamics, and provides sufficient conditions to certify signaling and temporal memory within OPT. As a concrete application of our OPT framework, we fully characterize the unique multi-time state in boxworld and develop a method for Bayesian retrodiction of physical transformations there. Our general framework is consistent with quantum theory, reproducing several existing results. In the non-Markovian quantum dynamics, we establish a correspondence between multi-time states and the process-matrix framework, and fully characterize the multi-time states compatible with general dynamics. This correspondence also lets us infer quantum causal models from multi-time states, and as a proof of principle, we propose a semidefinite program to infer causal order from quantum multi-time states. These results provide a unified framework for studying spatio-temporal states, causal relations, and Bayesian reasoning within OPTs, with implications for both fundamental and applied research.
tldr: The paper develops an axiomatic framework for multi-time states in operational probabilistic theories, covering Markovian and non-Markovian dynamics and connecting them to quantum process matrices and causal models.
motivation: Quantum states over time extend Bayesian reasoning to quantum theory and are useful for causality, open-system dynamics, and macroscopic realism, but a general axiomatic treatment beyond Markovian quantum mechanics was missing.
method: The authors introduce three assumptions—compositionality, reconstructibility, and spatio-temporal marginal consistency—to define multi-time states in a class of operational probabilistic theories that includes quantum mechanics as a special case.
result: They characterize multi-time states in boxworld, provide Bayesian retrodiction for transformations, show correspondence with the quantum process-matrix framework for non-Markovian dynamics, and propose a semidefinite program to infer causal order.
conclusion: The framework unifies spatio-temporal states, causal relations, and Bayesian reasoning across operational probabilistic theories, with implications for foundational and applied quantum information research.

The three axioms—compositionality (allowing composition of independent systems), reconstructibility (ensuring that states are determined by probabilities of outcomes of fiducial measurements), and spatio-temporal marginal consistency (ensuring that marginalizing over intermediate times yields valid multi-time states for the remaining times)—are used to derive the structure of multi-time states in general OPTs. The semidefinite program for causal order inference is formulated by casting the problem of finding a process matrix consistent with observed multi-time data as an SDP feasibility problem.

title: Ramp: Toward Ubiquitous Quantum-Safe Key Distribution As A Service
authors: Jiafan Wang, Sebastian Kish, Dongxi Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22879v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) offers a security foundation independent of computational hardness assumptions. However, its reliance on specialized hardware limits access by ordinary users. Turning QKD into a service poses a fundamental trust challenge, as the providers that supply QKD-derived material themselves could retain knowledge of the keying inputs of users. This makes end-to-end confidentiality solely depend on the trustworthiness of the service infrastructure. We present RAMP, a service-oriented framework that decouples QKD material generation from key consumption. Providers operate QKD infrastructure and supply raw-key materials, while users securely acquire, mask, and locally process them into final keys without operating QKD devices. RAMP employs reconciliation-preserving masking compatible with both DV- and CV-QKD. It mitigates the trust dependence by separating the QKD-service and user-side masking domains. We formalize complementary confidentiality guarantees: RAMP protects the final key even if colluding providers expose their complete raw-key views, provided the masking domain remains secure; conversely, exposing the complete masking state does not break final-key secrecy as long as the QKD source and acquisition paths remain protected. The results establish the dual-domain security boundary of RAMP. We implement RAMP using experimentally acquired QKD data and standardized quantum-safe cryptography. After acquiring service-provisioned keying material, commodity endpoints complete user-side QKD post-processing with an average key-distillation throughput of 2.1Kb/s on an M4 Pro CPU. To our knowledge, we demonstrate the first experimental realization of such service-provisioned, user-side QKD processing, presenting a viable path toward QKD as a service.
tldr: RAMP is a service-oriented QKD framework that separates provider-side raw-key generation from user-side key acquisition and masking, enabling QKD-derived keys to be delivered as a service with formal dual-domain confidentiality guarantees.
motivation: QKD offers security independent of computational assumptions, but specialized hardware limits ordinary-user access, and outsourcing QKD to providers creates a fundamental trust problem because providers may know the keying inputs.
method: The framework uses reconciliation-preserving masking compatible with both DV- and CV-QKD, lets providers supply raw-key material while users locally acquire, mask, and post-process it into final keys, and formalizes confidentiality under separate provider-side and user-side trust assumptions.

title: Programmable Preparation Of Topological Entangled States
authors: M. Javad Zakeri, Alaric Pan, Darren D Hudson, Andrea Blanco-Redondo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Programmable preparation of entangled quantum states is a central requirement for scalable quantum information processing, quantum networking and photonic quantum computing. Topological photonic platforms offer an attractive route towards robust quantum-state generation by encoding information in symmetry- protected optical modes, yet the generated entangled states are typically dictated by the lattice geometry and therefore lack programmability. Here we demonstrate programmable preparation of topological entangled states by inverse engineering the nonlinear optical pump profile of an integrated photonic lattice. Our approach enables deterministic control over both the dimensionality and modal structure of the generated entangled state while preserving its topological character. We experimentally realize silicon photonic topological superlattices in which the nonlinear generation pathway itself becomes programmable via tailored excitations. The superlattices host a multiband manifold of co localized topological interface modes, while coherently controlled inputs synthesize pump superpositions within this protected basis. We showcase this principle by selectively addressing topological biphoton eigenstates, steering correlations to produce a desired target state in a high-dimensional Hilbert space, and inverse-designing pump states that generate targeted Schmidt dimensionalities. Site-resolved two-photon correlation measurements remain reproducible across nominally identical fabricated devices, demonstrating robustness to realistic nanofabrication-induced disorder. Programmable preparation of topological entangled states establishes a pathway towards exploiting topological photonic modes as application-specific quantum resources, enabling tailored input states for high-dimensional quantum communication, quantum networking and photonic quantum computing.

method: The authors fabricate silicon photonic topological superlattices hosting co-localized interface modes and use coherently controlled pump superpositions to selectively address topological biphoton eigenstates and target Schmidt dimensionalities.
result: They achieve deterministic control over the dimensionality and modal structure of generated entangled states while preserving topological character, with reproducible site-resolved two-photon correlations across nominally identical devices.
conclusion: Programmable topological entangled-state preparation provides a route toward application-specific high-dimensional photonic resources for quantum communication, networking, and photonic quantum computing.

title: Quantumness Of Entanglement In Schwarzschild De Sitter Spacetime
authors: Xiaofen Huang Sumeng Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22761v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate genuine multipartite entanglement and genuine tripartite nonlocality of a noisy generalized GHZ state in Schwarzschild-de Sitter spacetime. The genuine multipartite concurrence and optimized Svetlichny parameter are employed to characterize these two quantum correlations. It is shown that the black hole and cosmological event horizons redistribute genuine multipartite entanglement differently among the physically accessible and inaccessible reduced states, while Svetlichny violation occurs only in the physically accessible state. We find that genuine multipartite entanglement can survive in the physically inaccessible states even when genuine tripartite nonlocality is absent. In addition, initial white noise suppresses both correlations, with Svetlichny nonlocality surviving over a narrower parameter region. Furthermore, in the Nariai limit, under the normalization adopted here, the correlations become concentrated in the physically accessible state. These results demonstrate the different robustness of genuine multipartite entanglement and genuine tripartite nonlocality under horizon effects and initial noise.

motivation: Understanding how black-hole and cosmological horizons affect multipartite quantum correlations is important for relativistic quantum information and for assessing the robustness of nonclassicality in curved spacetime.
method: The authors compute genuine multipartite concurrence and the optimized Svetlichny parameter for physically accessible and inaccessible reduced states of a noisy generalized GHZ state under Schwarzschild-de Sitter horizon effects.
result: They find that the two horizons redistribute genuine multipartite entanglement differently between accessible and inaccessible states, while Svetlichny nonlocality appears only in the physically accessible state; white noise suppresses both correlations, and in the Nariai limit correlations concentrate in the accessible state under their normalization.
conclusion: Genuine multipartite entanglement and genuine tripartite nonlocality exhibit different robustness under horizon effects and initial noise, with entanglement surviving in inaccessible states even when tripartite nonlocality is absent.

The authors consider a three-mode GHZ state initially shared by observers in the static region between the horizons, and then analyze the reduced states when one or more observers are in the physically inaccessible regions beyond the horizons. They employ the genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC) to quantify GME and the optimized Svetlichny parameter to characterize GTN. The results show that the two horizons redistribute GME differently among the accessible and inaccessible reduced states, while Svetlichny violation occurs only in the physically accessible state. Notably, GME can survive in the inaccessible states even when GTN is absent. Initial white noise suppresses both correlations, with Svetlichny nonlocality surviving over a narrower parameter region. In the Nariai limit (where the two horizons coincide), under their normalization, the correlations become concentrated in the physically accessible state. The study highlights the different robustness of GME and GTN under horizon effects and noise.

title: Encodings And Node Architecture: Lessons From The Fault-Tolerant Distributed Transversal Fanout
authors: Seng W. Loke
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An encoding choice specifies the quantum error-correcting code used to encode logical qubits at a given node. Different encoding choices may differ in the number of physical qubits, the number of encoded logical qubits, the code distance, and the available fault-tolerant operations. We study different encodings for a distributed transversal fanout operation and look at its implications on node architecture. Our experiments suggest that an encoding with higher distance, even if requiring more ebits, can yield a lower logical error rate for distributed operations, and that ``upgrading'' an encoding prior to distributed operations and having a cache, as part of node architecture, for qubits can be useful for distributed operations.

result: Their experiments suggest that higher-distance encodings can yield lower logical error rates for distributed operations even when more ebits are required, and that upgrading encodings before distributed operations plus caching qubits can be beneficial.
conclusion: Encoding and node-architecture co-design matter for fault-tolerant distributed quantum operations, with distance and caching/upgrade strategies playing important roles.

title: Resonant Pair Production And Flat Band Melting In A Driven Rydberg Chain
authors: K. Sengupta Tista Banerjee
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study a Rydberg chain subjected to a two-tone periodic drive of the detuning [MATH] and Rabi frequency [MATH] at frequencies [MATH] and [MATH] respectively with [MATH]. In the strong Rydberg blockade limit, such a system reduces to the PXP model and exhibits exact Floquet flat band. Here we determine, using a time-dependent Schrieffer-Wolff transformation, the domain of validity of such PXP dynamics once the blockade-violating processes are taken into account. We study the melting of such flat bands in the presence of strong, but finite, blockade strength. Using Floquet perturbation theory (FPT), we identify two mechanisms for such melting; the first occurs due to the presence of many-body resonances involving resonant production of nearest-neighbor Rydberg excitation pairs while the second involves virtual processes that access intermediate states with such pairs. Our analytical FPT results match with those obtained using exact diagonalization on a finite chain. We study the dynamics for [MATH] (Fock state with no Rydberg excitation), [MATH], and [MATH] (Fock states with Rydberg excitations on alternate and every third site respectively) initial states. We find that [MATH] shows exceptional stability against resonant pair formation while [MATH] exhibits flat band melting via virtual processes away from the direct resonances. We find oscillatory dynamics with large time period for the [MATH] initial state and the presence of Floquet scars that have large overlap with [MATH] state; these phenomena occur due to processes that are absent in the PXP limit. We propose measurement of nearest neighbor pair correlation functions using Rydberg atom quantum simulator platforms as an accessible experimental probe for these effects.

title: Quantum-Assisted Unambiguous Discrimination Of Pure States With Robustness Bounds
authors: Jinhyeok Heo, Dongkeun Lee, Junghee Ryu, Minjin Choi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a hybrid quantum-classical framework for the unambiguous discrimination of pure states by combining the noisy intermediate-scale quantum semidefinite program solver (NSS) with the reciprocal-state representation. In NSS, a given semidefinite program (SDP) is represented within a subspace spanned by chosen ansatz states, with the required quantities estimated using quantum circuits, and the resulting optimization is performed classically. This makes NSS naturally applicable to discrimination problems involving circuit-prepared states, as finding a discrimination measurement can be formulated as an SDP. By choosing the discriminated states themselves as the ansatz and exploiting the reciprocal-state representation, the general matrix-variable NSS formulation is reduced to an optimization over N scalar variables, where N is the number of discriminated states. The resulting formulation reduces the number of optimization variables and positive-semidefinite constraints compared with the original NSS formulation. We further establish robustness guarantees against Gram matrix estimation errors, including a rescaling procedure that guarantees a valid positive operator-valued measure (POVM) under bounded perturbations. The resulting bounds quantify both the deviation in average success probability and violations of the no-error condition using only the estimated Gram matrix, its SDP solution, and a characterized perturbation bound, without access to the ideal Gram matrix. Numerical simulations validate the derived robustness bounds and characterize finite-shot scaling. We also perform experiments on IBM quantum hardware to estimate pairwise overlaps, and then evaluate the performance of the resulting POVMs.
tldr: A hybrid quantum-classical framework for unambiguous discrimination of pure states using a NISQ SDP solver and reciprocal-state representation, with robustness bounds against Gram matrix estimation errors.
motivation: Unambiguous discrimination of nonorthogonal pure states is a fundamental quantum information primitive, but practical NISQ implementations require reduced optimization overhead and robustness to noisy overlap estimation.
method: The authors combine the NISQ semidefinite program solver with the reciprocal-state representation, reducing the general matrix-variable SDP to an optimization over N scalar variables, and derive robustness guarantees for the resulting POVM under bounded Gram matrix perturbations.
result: They establish bounds on deviations in average success probability and violations of the no-error condition using only the estimated Gram matrix, its SDP solution, and a perturbation bound, and validate the approach with numerical simulations and IBM quantum hardware experiments estimating pairwise overlaps.
conclusion: The framework provides a resource-efficient and robust route to quantum-assisted unambiguous state discrimination on near-term devices, though its contribution is primarily methodological and applied rather than a new information-theoretic result.

title: Discrete Time Crystals And Classical Logic Gates In Coupled Open Dicke Models
authors: Emmanuel D. G. U, Roy D. Jara Jr., Jayson G. Cosme
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the dynamics of coupled discrete time crystals (DTCs) in the coupled Dicke model or Dicke dimer (DD) with dissipation. By numerically simulating the mean-field dynamics of the system, we show that coupling two DTCs decreases their oscillation amplitude following a transient relaxation period. For sufficiently strong coupling, the coupled DTCs become unstable, resulting in the system relaxing towards the normal phase (NP). We demonstrate that the relaxation time diverges near the critical coupling strength, suggesting a continuous phase transition. Using the truncated Wigner approximation (TWA), we explore how the dynamics are affected by the introduction of quantum fluctuations. We also consider a scenario in which an NP is briefly coupled to a DTC, seeding the NP to transform into a DTC that is either synchronized or anti-synchronized relative to the DTC. We investigate the robustness of this phenomenon in the presence of noise. Using these results, we propose a scheme to perform NAND and NOR operations with three DTCs by sequentially coupling the input and output sites. We identify the parameter regimes in which the logic gate architecture remains valid, and investigate how the protocol is affected by the presence of quantum fluctuations.

method: The authors numerically simulate mean-field dynamics of the coupled Dicke model with dissipation and use the truncated Wigner approximation to include quantum fluctuations and noise.
result: They find that coupling two DTCs reduces oscillation amplitude and can drive the system to the normal phase beyond a critical coupling, with a diverging relaxation time; they then show NAND/NOR operations can be implemented in certain parameter regimes.
conclusion: The work suggests that coupled DTCs in Dicke-type hybrid systems could serve as building blocks for classical logic, though quantum fluctuations constrain the viable parameter regimes.

title: Liouvillian Non-Invertible Symmetry
authors: Ying-Cheng Yang, Jhen-Dong Lin, Yueh-Nan Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23111v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-invertible symmetries extend conventional symmetries beyond group-like transformations and play an important role in quantum field theory and many-body physics. However, a general framework of non-invertible symmetries in open quantum systems is still lacking. Here, we formulate a general Liouville-space duality framework that extends Hilbert-space non-invertible dualities to open quantum systems. The resulting defect relates Liouvillians with dual Hamiltonian and dissipative parameters and becomes an exact symmetry at self-duality. We apply this framework to the periodic transverse-field Ising chain with two collective Lindblad channels exchanged by Kramers--Wannier (KW) duality. A strong [MATH] symmetry divides Liouville space into four parity sectors, while the defect acts nontrivially only in the even-even sector. At self-duality, the KW defect imposes a momentum-resolved selection rule on Liouvillian Jordan blocks. Modes with different Liouville momenta or KW-defect eigenvalues cannot form a common exceptional Jordan block. For a three-site chain, a global R\'enyi-2 KW asymmetry dynamically identifies the self-dual conditions. At the same time, the spectral structure exhibits both a semisimple degeneracy and a self-dual exceptional point with a perturbation-selective response. These results extend non-invertible dualities to Markovian quantum dynamics and establish a symmetry-based selection rule for Liouvillian Jordan structures.
tldr: The paper develops a Liouville-space duality framework for non-invertible symmetries in open quantum systems and applies it to a dissipative transverse-field Ising chain.
motivation: Non-invertible symmetries are well developed in closed quantum systems, but a general framework for open quantum systems is lacking.
method: The authors formulate a Liouville-space duality that relates Liouvillians with dual Hamiltonian and dissipative parameters, and apply it to a periodic transverse-field Ising chain with two collective Lindblad channels exchanged by Kramers-Wannier duality.
result: They identify parity sectors, derive a momentum-resolved selection rule for Liouvillian Jordan blocks at self-duality, and show that a Rényi-2 asymmetry dynamically identifies self-dual conditions in a three-site chain.
conclusion: The work extends non-invertible dualities to Markovian quantum dynamics and establishes symmetry-based constraints on Liouvillian spectral structure.

title: The Classical Boundary Of Quantum Computation: History-Resolved Causal Stochastic Machines And The Cost Of Classicalization
authors: Kyoungho Cho, Junghee Ryu, Minsu Kim, Jeongho Bang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22750v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What separates quantum computation from classical computation when a classical model may retain every branch history and arbitrary causal memory? We study this question using history-resolved causal stochastic machines (HCSMs), which describe positive causal history laws. Probabilistic Turing machines (PTMs) embed in stochastic-ensemble models (SEnMs), which in turn embed in HCSMs. We prove that HCSM history laws coincide exactly with the fixed-basis, prefix-preserving diagonal sector of ideal quantum processes, denoted by [MATH] and distinguished here from algorithmic quantum Turing machines (QTMs). Coherent quantum processes extend strictly beyond this sector. The boundary is already visible in reversibility. Born-probability shadows of unitary gates preserve inverse composition exactly for basis permutations with phases. Outside this class, an exact positive stochastic simulation that supports universal quantum continuations must retain predictive information absent from visible probabilities. An inverse-recovery identity quantifies this phase ledger, and universal continuation forces the retained probability law to be tomographically sufficient for the quantum state. Under continuous full-state encoding assumptions, this requirement yields quantum-state dimension lower bounds. The familiar slogan [MATH] is thereby sharpened into a precise classical boundary and a no-free-classicalization principle. Complete classical branching does not remove the predictive information needed to represent quantum coherence.
tldr: The paper defines a precise classical boundary for quantum computation using history-resolved causal stochastic machines and shows that classical branching cannot eliminate the predictive information needed to represent quantum coherence.
motivation: It asks what fundamentally separates quantum from classical computation when classical models are allowed arbitrary causal memory and full branch histories.
method: The authors introduce history-resolved causal stochastic machines, compare them with probabilistic Turing machines and quantum Turing machines, and analyze Born-probability shadows of unitary gates via inverse-recovery identities.
result: They prove HCSM history laws coincide only with a fixed-basis prefix-preserving diagonal sector of ideal quantum processes, while coherent processes require retained predictive information and imply quantum-state dimension lower bounds under full-state encoding.
conclusion: The work sharpens the classical-quantum boundary into a no-free-classicalization principle: complete classical branching still cannot remove the hidden predictive information required for quantum coherence.

title: Quantum-Classical Neural Networks For Solving Lindblad Master Equations
authors: Rafael Florencio D\'iaz, Julio Guerrero Garc\'ia, Elvira Romera Guti\'errez
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22691v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational quantum algorithms have emerged as a promising approach for simulating open quantum systems, yet their expressive power and trainability remain poorly understood. We propose a variational framework for solving Lindblad master equations by minimizing a residual cost function using a compositional ansatz obtained by combining a classical neural network with a parameterized quantum circuit. The density matrix is represented through a purification on an enlarged Hilbert space, ensuring positivity, Hermiticity, and unit trace by construction, while all gradients are evaluated exactly via the parameter-shift rule. Beyond the algorithmic formulation, we derive an upper bound for the covering number of the proposed compositional model and compare it with that of purely quantum neural networks. Our analysis shows that the classical parametrization enlarges the effective hypothesis class while providing finer control over its complexity, thereby establishing a theoretical connection between expressivity, covering numbers, effective dimension, and the barren plateau phenomenon. Numerical experiments validate both the accuracy of the proposed method for representative Lindblad master equations and the theoretical predictions regarding gradient concentration. These results provide a unified variational and theoretical framework for the simulation of dissipative quantum dynamics using compositional quantum machine learning models.
tldr: The paper proposes a compositional classical-neural-network plus parameterized-quantum-circuit variational ansatz for solving Lindblad master equations and analyzes its expressivity and trainability via covering numbers and barren-plateau behavior.
motivation: Variational quantum algorithms are promising for simulating open quantum systems, but their expressive power and trainability remain poorly understood. The authors aim to improve both the practical solver and the theoretical understanding of hybrid quantum-classical models.
method: The density matrix is represented by purification on an enlarged Hilbert space, ensuring physical consistency, while gradients are computed exactly with the parameter-shift rule. The authors derive a covering-number upper bound for the hybrid model and compare it with purely quantum neural networks, supported by numerical experiments on representative Lindblad equations.
result: The classical parametrization is shown to enlarge the effective hypothesis class while allowing finer control of model complexity, connecting expressivity, covering numbers, effective dimension, and barren plateaus. Numerical experiments validate the solver's accuracy and the predicted gradient-concentration behavior.
conclusion: The work provides a unified variational and theoretical framework for simulating dissipative quantum dynamics with compositional quantum machine-learning models, though its primary contribution is in quantum machine learning rather than the researcher's core information-theoretic or thermodynamic interests.

title: A Thermally And Perturbatively Stable Classical Spin Model In Two Dimensions
authors: Shankar Balasubramanian, Margarita Davydova, Ting-Chun Lin, Ryan Thorngren
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22548v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that the 2D classical spin model constructed in arXiv:2605.10943 hosts many metastable states at non-zero temperature which are stable to arbitrary Hamiltonian perturbations, providing the first such example. Our proof relies on a recursive application of the cluster expansion.
tldr: The authors prove that a previously constructed 2D classical spin model has many thermally metastable states that remain stable under arbitrary Hamiltonian perturbations, using a recursive cluster expansion.
motivation: The work aims to establish the first example of a two-dimensional classical spin model with metastable states at nonzero temperature that are robust to arbitrary Hamiltonian perturbations.
method: The proof recursively applies the cluster expansion to analyze the stability of metastable states against perturbations.
result: The model hosts many metastable states at nonzero temperature, and these states are stable to arbitrary Hamiltonian perturbations.
conclusion: This provides a rigorous example of perturbatively stable thermal metastability in a 2D classical spin system, with potential implications for understanding stability in statistical mechanics.

title: Nonequilibrium Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions In The Extended Agassi Model
authors: Ritesh Kumar Palai, Rajiv Kumar, Venktesh Singh, Sunil K. Mishra
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in the extended Agassi model following sudden quenches of same level pairing ([MATH]), monopole-monopole ([MATH]) and cross level pairing ([MATH]) strengths. Using exact diagonalization, we characterize the non-equilibrium dynamics through the Loschmidt echo and intensive return-rate function. Quenches across equilibrium phase boundaries produce cusp-like structures in the return rate that shows non-analyticities with increasing system size. Equilibrium finite size to large scaling identifies the [MATH]-driven transition as a second order phase transition similar to mean-field, Dicke, and Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick (LMG) models critical behaviour with the exponent of the order parameter [MATH], while the [MATH]- and [MATH]-driven transitions are first order. We further characterize the associated dynamical singularities through a local scaling exponent [MATH], with [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] of all three parameters. The distinct scaling behaviours across the parameter channels show that dynamical criticality is not determined solely by the equilibrium order of the transition, revealing multiple dynamical scaling regimes. These non-analyticities are associated with the Fisher zeros of the Loschmidt amplitude, which cross the real time axis at critical times and the time derivatives of the return-rate function to characterize the order of DQPTs within the extended Agassi model.
tldr: The paper studies dynamical quantum phase transitions in the extended Agassi model after sudden quenches by analyzing the Loschmidt echo, return rate, and Fisher zeros.
motivation: It aims to understand how nonequilibrium criticality in a many-body model depends on quench parameters and whether it is dictated by the equilibrium order of the transition.
method: Using exact diagonalization, the authors perform sudden quenches in pairing, monopole-monopole, and cross-level pairing strengths and extract nonanalyticities via the return-rate function, finite-size scaling, local scaling exponents, and Fisher zeros.
result: The monopole-monopole-driven transition is found to be second order with mean-field-like exponent, while the pairing and cross-level pairing transitions are first order; distinct dynamical scaling exponents are obtained for the three channels.
conclusion: Dynamical criticality is not determined solely by the equilibrium transition order, revealing multiple dynamical scaling regimes and characterizing DQPT order through return-rate time derivatives.

title: Exploring Quantum Phase Transitions Beyond Landau Theory On A Quantum Processor
authors: Ruizhe Shen, Yin Zhong, Ching Hua Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22482v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Direct continuous quantum phase transitions between phases that break distinct symmetries challenge the conventional Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm and provide a framework for deconfined quantum criticality. Here, we investigate a Landau-forbidden ferromagnetic-to-valence-bond-solid (FM-VBS) transition in a frustrated one-dimensional spin chain using superconducting quantum processors. Combining matrix-product-state-assisted circuit preparation with quantum-hardware measurements, we resolve the suppression of long-range ferromagnetic correlations and the redistribution of competing-order fluctuations across the transition. Distance-resolved correlations and finite-size analyses reveal signatures consistent with critical behavior. We further extend our investigation to nonequilibrium dynamics, directly preparing dimerized states and tracking the evolution of VBS order and joint FM-VBS fluctuations under local unitary interactions. Our results establish a versatile quantum-hardware framework for probing competing orders, critical correlations, and many-body dynamics beyond conventional Landau theory.
tldr: A superconducting-quantum-processor study of a Landau-forbidden ferromagnetic-to-valence-bond-solid transition in a frustrated spin chain, probing critical correlations and nonequilibrium dynamics.
motivation: Direct continuous transitions between phases breaking distinct symmetries challenge the Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson paradigm and offer a route to deconfined quantum criticality, motivating hardware-based exploration of such Landau-forbidden critical points.
method: Matrix-product-state-assisted circuit preparation combined with measurements on superconducting quantum processors, using distance-resolved correlations and finite-size scaling, plus quench-type evolution of dimerized states under local unitaries.
result: The experiments resolve suppression of long-range ferromagnetic correlations and redistribution of competing-order fluctuations across the transition, with signatures consistent with critical behavior, and track VBS order and joint FM-VBS fluctuations out of equilibrium.
conclusion: The work establishes a quantum-hardware framework for probing competing orders and many-body dynamics beyond conventional Landau theory.

title: Two-photon Doppler-free Spectroscopy Of The $6s^2\;^1S_0 \rightarrow 6s23s\;^1S_0$ Rydberg Transition For Quantum Sensing In Ytterbium
authors: Benjamin D. Hunt, Kyle Beloy, Roger C. Brown, Tobias Bothwell, Harikesh Ranganath, Tanner Grogan, Jacob L. Siegel, Andrew Ludlow
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Here we report atomic structure calculations and experimental observations of the two-photon [MATH] transition in Yb. The unique level structure of Yb places the [MATH] state's energy at [MATH] of the ionization energy, which facilitates two-photon Doppler-free excitation of the [MATH] Rydberg state from the [MATH] ground state at a relatively low optical intensity. This [MATH] transition is immune to first-order Zeeman and electric quadrupole shifts, has reduced sensitivity to higher-order Zeeman shifts, and is further predicted to have relatively low sensitivity to density shifts. Using configuration interaction theory, we compute relevant properties of the [MATH] Rydberg state for sensing, including the [MATH] coefficient, dc polarizability, blackbody radiation (BBR) shift, and BBR depopulation rate. As a first experimental step, we demonstrate two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of the [MATH] transition. From our experimental spectra, we estimate the natural linewidth (lifetime) of the [MATH] state to be 90 kHz (1.8 [MATH]s). We believe this transition, or other [MATH] transitions in Yb with [MATH], may find use in a variety of sensing applications, potentially including a two-photon clock, electrometer, or BBR thermometer.
tldr: The paper reports atomic-structure calculations and two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy of a Yb Rydberg transition for quantum sensing applications.
motivation: Yb has a favorable level structure enabling low-intensity two-photon Doppler-free excitation of a Rydberg state with reduced sensitivity to several systematic shifts, making it attractive for precision sensing.
method: Configuration-interaction calculations are used to compute sensing-relevant properties of the excited Rydberg state, and two-photon Doppler-free spectroscopy is performed experimentally.
result: The authors compute the relevant coefficient, dc polarizability, blackbody-radiation shift, and depopulation rate, and from measured spectra estimate a natural linewidth of 90 kHz, corresponding to a 1.8 microsecond lifetime.
conclusion: The transition is proposed as a candidate for applications such as a two-photon clock, electrometer, or blackbody-radiation thermometer.

title: Circuit Synthesis For Variational Quantum Algorithms: The Depth Of Algebra And Geometry
authors: Boris Tsvelikhovskiy
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22689v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The analysis of Hamiltonian Variational Ans\"atze centers on three fundamental questions: which states are exactly reachable from a given initial state, what native control depth suffices for local and global synthesis, and whether a bounded circuit extension can expose a direction of decreasing cost at a suboptimal output. We address these challenges by leveraging the dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) associated with the circuits and the geometry of the initial state's orbit under the action of the corresponding dynamical Lie group [MATH]. We show that an initial state has a closed projective orbit whenever it is a nondegenerate eigenstate of a control Hamiltonian. Combined with asymptotic QAOA convergence, this guarantees exact, finite depth ground state preparation for architectures employing diagonal problem Hamiltonians and irreducible stoquastic mixers. We bound the number of native control exponentials required for local unitary synthesis and state preparation using DLA commutator filtration growth alongside reachable orbit dimensions. Complementing these local results, we construct global frameworks on invariant sectors equipped with full unitary or special unitary dynamical Lie algebras. These constructions yield explicit applications to Pauli-generated systems and constrained maximum independent set multi-angle QAOA circuits; specifically, we show that their native control costs are directly determined by commutator filtration depth and independent-set toggle-group geometry, respectively. Finally, if the dynamical Lie group is compact, the observable [MATH] generates an admissible evolution ([MATH], where [MATH] is the DLA), and the projective orbit of the initial state contains a ground state ray of [MATH], then a bounded depth, identity-initialized circuit extension exhibits either first-order descent or negative curvature at every suboptimal circuit output.
tldr: The paper uses dynamical Lie algebras and orbit geometry to analyze reachability, control depth, and synthesis guarantees for Hamiltonian variational ansätze and QAOA-style circuits.
motivation: Variational quantum algorithms require a principled understanding of which states are reachable, how much control depth is needed, and whether circuit extensions can guarantee cost improvement at suboptimal points.
method: The author studies the dynamical Lie algebra of the circuit and the geometry of the initial state's orbit under the dynamical Lie group, bounding synthesis costs via commutator filtration growth and reachable orbit dimensions.
result: The paper proves finite-depth exact ground-state preparation for certain QAOA architectures, derives native control-cost bounds for local and global synthesis, and shows that compact dynamical Lie groups yield bounded-depth circuit extensions with first-order descent or negative curvature at every suboptimal output.
conclusion: The algebraic and geometric framework provides rigorous circuit-synthesis guarantees for variational quantum algorithms, with explicit applications to Pauli-generated systems and constrained maximum independent set QAOA circuits.

title: Sample-Based Quantum Linear Solver And Bounds On Krylov-State Sampling
authors: Byeongyong Park, Keunhong Jeong, Doyeol Ahn
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23138v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: To solve linear systems [MATH], we propose a sample-based quantum linear solver combining quantum Krylov-state sampling with classical variational diagonalization. Rather than simulating the cost Hamiltonian [MATH], we measure quantum Krylov states [MATH] generated by the original Hermitian operator [MATH] in the computational basis. We then classically diagonalize the projected cost Hamiltonian to reconstruct an approximate solution. Using a representation of [MATH] as a linear combination of quantum Krylov states, we derive lower bounds on computational-basis sampling probabilities from solution amplitudes. We establish support-discovery guarantees for finite nonnegative-time grid sampling and signed-time sampling, which permits both positive and negative evolution times. The former bounds the maximum evolution time, whereas the latter improves ideal shot complexity at the cost of occasional long evolutions. For a condition-number bound [MATH] on [MATH], a lower bound [MATH] on the solution probability weight of each of [MATH] target basis states, and failure probability [MATH], signed-time sampling achieves [MATH] shots, matching a worst-case lower bound up to constants within an evolution-only observation model in a specified parameter regime. Finally, we analyze the effects of finite-length qDRIFT compilation and circuit reuse on sampling and derive an infidelity bound for the reconstructed solution.
tldr: Proposes a sample-based quantum linear solver that combines quantum Krylov-state sampling with classical variational diagonalization and derives sampling-complexity guarantees.
motivation: To solve linear systems without simulating the cost Hamiltonian directly, the authors use quantum Krylov states generated by the original Hermitian operator and reconstruct solutions via classical diagonalization.
method: The protocol measures quantum Krylov states in the computational basis, classically diagonalizes the projected cost Hamiltonian, and derives lower bounds on sampling probabilities plus support-discovery guarantees for finite nonnegative-time and signed-time grid sampling.
result: Signed-time sampling achieves a shot complexity matching a worst-case lower bound up to constants within a specified observation model, and the paper bounds solution infidelity under finite-length qDRIFT compilation and circuit reuse.
conclusion: The work provides theoretical guarantees for a sample-based quantum linear solver, but it is an algorithms/sampling-complexity contribution rather than a core result in the researcher's priority areas.

title: Aligning Information Theory And Formal Verification: A Lean Formalization Of Rate-Distortion Theory
authors: Fubin Yan, Ruxuan Dong, Ruoxuan Shi, Duolei Wang, Kenneth W. Shum
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22404v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models have recently demonstrated an ability to generate substantial mathematical proofs and formalizations, including machine-checked arguments for major open problems and classical theorems. These developments highlight a growing workflow in which AI systems search for proofs while proof assistants certify their correctness. Within information theory, however, formalized libraries remain limited, and existing formalized theorems focus almost exclusively on Shannon's foundational lossless theorems. This paper presents the first Lean formalization of core components of rate-distortion theory, a central framework for lossy compression and modern machine-learning analysis. We identify the alignment challenges that arise when translating information-theoretic definitions, such as distortion measures, typicality and achievability, into a proof-assistant setting, and we develop a reusable library of definitions and lemmas faithful to textbook conventions. Our formalization provides a foundation for future AI-assisted proofs in information theory and enables subsequent mechanized developments to build on a coherent, verified infrastructure rather than generating long proofs from scratch.
tldr: The paper presents the first Lean formalization of core rate-distortion theory, covering distortion measures, typicality, and achievability, with a reusable verified library.
motivation: Formalized libraries in information theory are sparse and mostly limited to Shannon's lossless theorems, while AI-generated proofs increasingly need machine-checked certification; lossy compression theory lacks such infrastructure.
method: The authors translate textbook definitions of rate-distortion theory into Lean, identifying alignment challenges in encoding distortion measures, typicality, and achievability arguments, and build a library of faithful definitions and lemmas.
result: A coherent, machine-checked Lean library formalizing key components of rate-distortion theory is produced, along with a discussion of the conceptual mismatches encountered in formalization.
conclusion: The work provides foundational infrastructure for AI-assisted and mechanized proofs in information theory, enabling future formal developments to build on verified components rather than starting from scratch.

title: Gaussian Identification In Mimo Channels
authors: Christian Deppe Mohammad Javad Salariseddigh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22931v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the identification capacity of discrete-time Gaussian multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) channels under per-antenna, per-symbol peak-amplitude constraints. We establish upper and lower bounds on the identification capacity that scale linearly with the channel rank [MATH] The number of reliably identifiable messages can grow super-exponentially with blocklength [MATH] following [MATH] where [MATH] is an achievable rate. The channel rank provides a spatial-multiplexing advantage, enabling higher achievable rates and, consequently, stronger super-exponential codebook growth. These results characterize the rank-dependent gain in achievable identification performance.
tldr: The paper derives upper and lower bounds on the identification capacity of discrete-time Gaussian MIMO channels under per-antenna peak-amplitude constraints, showing rank-linear scaling and super-exponential message growth.
motivation: Identification capacity — the number of messages a receiver can identify rather than decode — is a classical information-theoretic problem, and characterizing it for realistic constrained Gaussian MIMO channels is the gap the authors address.
method: The authors derive coding theorems: converse (upper) bounds and achievability (lower) bounds for identification over MIMO Gaussian channels with per-antenna, per-symbol peak-amplitude constraints, expressing the achievable identification rate in terms of channel rank.
result: The identification capacity scales linearly with channel rank, and the number of reliably identifiable messages grows super-exponentially in blocklength as 2^{2^{nR}} with R an achievable rate that increases with spatial multiplexing.
conclusion: Channel rank supplies a spatial-multiplexing advantage that strengthens super-exponential codebook growth, quantifying rank-dependent gains in identification performance.

title: Unconditional Quantum Pac Learning Advantage In The Large Error Regime
authors: Igor C. Oliveira
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23268v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish an unconditional super-polynomial separation between quantum and classical PAC learning of Boolean functions under the uniform distribution in the large error regime. For every advantage [MATH], we construct a concept class that a polynomial-time quantum learner learns to agreement [MATH] with success probability at least [MATH]. The learner uses only quantum random examples and outputs a polynomial-size deterministic classical circuit. In contrast, no polynomial-time classical learner achieves agreement [MATH] with success probability greater than [MATH], even with membership queries. To achieve this, we develop a nearly-optimal quantum learner that uses quantum random examples to produce a hypothesis achieving a prescribed correlation with an arbitrary Boolean function. The learner generalizes Fourier sampling from parity hypotheses to quadratic hypotheses. While standard Fourier sampling is insensitive to the sign of the correlation, we use interference to bias sampling toward positively correlated hypotheses. This is combined with a careful analysis of the resulting distribution to boost both the learner's success probability and its agreement with the target function. We believe that the resulting quantum learning algorithm might be of independent interest. Finally, although a robust quantum PAC learning advantage holds unconditionally in the large error regime, we note that an analogous separation between quantum and classical learning in the small error regime would imply that [MATH].
tldr: The paper proves an unconditional super-polynomial separation between quantum and classical PAC learning of Boolean functions under the uniform distribution in the large-error regime.
motivation: Quantum PAC learning advantages were previously known only under cryptographic or complexity-theoretic assumptions, or in restricted error regimes; the author asks whether an unconditional separation can be established.
method: A polynomial-time quantum learner using quantum random examples is constructed by generalizing Fourier sampling from parity to quadratic hypotheses, exploiting interference to bias sampling toward positively correlated hypotheses, plus a distributional analysis boosting success probability and agreement.
result: For every advantage, a concept class exists that a quantum learner learns to the prescribed agreement with high probability while no polynomial-time classical learner (even with membership queries) can exceed a strictly smaller agreement; the analogous small-error separation would imply a complexity-theoretic consequence.
conclusion: A robust unconditional quantum learning advantage holds in the large-error regime, and the proposed interference-based learning algorithm may be of independent interest.

title: Single-Letterization Of Rate-Cost Tradeoffs In Static Time-Invariant Control (stic) Systems
authors: Eray Unsal Atay, Venkat Chandrasekaran, Victoria Kostina
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22789v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In settings such as online recommendation platforms, medical decision-making with interim summaries, and stochastic control with static plants, the underlying system is often static so that the next state depends only on the most recent action. Moreover, the true system state is high-dimensional and cannot be observed directly, so actions must be selected based on information received through a rate-limited communication link, which constrains the control performance. This leads to a fundamental rate-cost tradeoff[MATH]the minimum communication rate required to achieve a prescribed average control cost. We study this tradeoff for a class of static systems we term static time-invariant control (STIC) systems, namely, control systems in which the next state depends on the history only through the most recent control action via a time-invariant kernel. For general control systems[MATH]not necessarily static or time-invariant[MATH]our prior work characterized this tradeoff through the limit of a sequence of directed-information minimization problems. However, the dimension of these problems grows with the time horizon, making the limiting formulation computationally intractable. In the present paper, we show for STIC systems that this growing-size formulation admits a single-letter characterization. This identifies STIC systems as the control-side counterpart of Noisy Output is the STate (NOST) channels[MATH]one of the few channel models whose feedback capacity admits a single-letter characterization. This yields, to our knowledge, the first constant-size convex characterization of the rate[MATH]cost tradeoff beyond linear quadratic Gaussian (LQG) control.
tldr: The paper derives a single-letter characterization of the rate-cost tradeoff for static time-invariant control systems with rate-limited communication.
motivation: Rate-limited control systems often require computationally intractable multi-letter characterizations of the fundamental communication-rate versus control-cost tradeoff.
method: The authors specialize a directed-information minimization framework to static time-invariant control (STIC) systems and prove that the limiting formulation admits a constant-size single-letter convex characterization.
result: STIC systems are identified as the control-side counterpart of NOST channels, yielding the first constant-size convex characterization of the rate-cost tradeoff beyond LQG control.
conclusion: The work provides a tractable information-theoretic characterization for a broad class of static control systems, but it is purely classical and does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Thermalization-induced Self-polarization Of Temporally Incoherent Light: A Nonequilibrium Wave Turbulence Kinetic Approach
authors: L. Zanaglia, J. Garnier, M. Ferraro, T. Torres, C. Michel, V. Doya, G. Millot, S. Wabnitz, I. Carusotto, A. Picozzi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conservative nonlinear waves generally undergo an irreversible process of thermalization toward the Rayleigh--Jeans (RJ) equilibrium state. Light thermalization has recently been experimentally investigated in the two-dimensional transverse spatial dynamics of multimode waveguides.
