Here, we consider the one-dimensional temporal dynamics of incoherent light propagating in a weakly birefringent single-mode fiber. We show that light thermalization is responsible for a self-polarization of the incoherent wave during its propagation. Within the framework of wave turbulence theory, we show that this phenomenon originates from a nonequilibrium process of adiabatic cooling: polarization fluctuations are continuously transferred toward the high-frequency tails of a local RJ equilibrium state, whose effective temperature decreases during propagation, thereby increasing the degree of light polarization. Moreover, in the absence of a high-frequency cut-off that would regularize the ultraviolet catastrophe in the temporal domain, the optical wave exhibits an ever-increasing degree of polarization, ultimately approaching unity. These results show that it is thermodynamically advantageous for the optical field to evolve toward a polarized state, which provides new insight into spontaneous self-organization phenomena in conservative Hamiltonian systems operating far from thermodynamic equilibrium.
tldr: The paper develops a nonequilibrium wave-turbulence kinetic theory showing that thermalization of temporally incoherent light in a weakly birefringent fiber causes self-polarization via adiabatic cooling.
motivation: Conservative nonlinear waves tend to thermalize toward Rayleigh-Jeans equilibrium, and recent experiments have studied this in spatial multimode waveguide dynamics; the authors ask whether analogous thermalization affects the temporal polarization dynamics of incoherent light in a single-mode fiber.
method: They use wave turbulence theory to describe the one-dimensional temporal evolution of incoherent light in a weakly birefringent fiber, tracking polarization fluctuations and their transfer toward high-frequency tails of a local Rayleigh-Jeans equilibrium.
result: Thermalization induces self-polarization because polarization fluctuations are transferred to high-frequency modes while the local effective temperature decreases; without a high-frequency cutoff, the degree of polarization increases indefinitely toward unity.
conclusion: The optical field finds it thermodynamically advantageous to evolve toward a polarized state, providing insight into spontaneous self-organization in conservative Hamiltonian systems far from equilibrium.

title: A Generalized Half-Singleton Bound For List Decoding Of Insertion/Deletion Errors
authors: Neehar Verma, Camilla Hollanti, Razane Tajeddine
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23270v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We derive an upper bound on the rate of a linear code capable of list decoding from insertion and deletion errors. Subsequently, we show that a linear code can list decode from at most [MATH] insdel errors with fixed list size [MATH], and that this bound is strict when the code does not contain the all-ones vector. We also provide a simple construction of codes achieving the optimal rate for any given list size capable of correcting a single insdel error. All the results hold for linear codes over finite fields of size [MATH].
tldr: The paper derives a generalized half-Singleton upper bound on the rate of linear codes for list decoding insertion/deletion errors and constructs optimal single-error-correcting codes.
motivation: List decoding of insertion/deletion errors is important in coding theory, but existing bounds are limited; the authors aim to generalize the half-Singleton bound to this setting.
method: They prove an upper bound on the code rate for list decoding insdel errors and show strictness under certain conditions, then give a construction achieving optimal rate for single insdel error correction with arbitrary list size.
result: A linear code can list decode from at most a certain number of insdel errors with fixed list size, with a strict bound when the code lacks the all-ones vector; explicit optimal-rate codes for one insdel error are provided.
conclusion: The work extends classical coding bounds to list decoding of insertion/deletion errors, but remains purely classical and does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Ultra-stable Laser With sub-Hz Intrinsic Linewidth Using A Silicon Photonic Chip
authors: Mohamad Hossein Idjadi, Haotian Cheng, Benjia Li, Tzu-Yung Huang, Kwangwoong Kim, Naijun Jin, Peter T. Rakich
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Here, we demonstrate a novel optical self-injection-locking scheme integrated with a modulation-free laser frequency stabilization technique co-integrated with a compact vacuum-gap micro-Fabry-Perot cavity (uFP), with Q-factor of 3.46E9, to realize an ultra-stable laser with sub-Hz fundamental linewidth using a silicon photonic chip. The demonstrated electro-optic self-injection locking (EOSIL) chip suppresses a commercial DFB diode laser's frequency noise power spectral density by more than 110 dB at 1 Hz offset, approaching the theoretical thermal noise limit of the uFP cavity, and enables a laser fundamental linewidth of 58 mHz with a fractional frequency instability of 8.68E-13 at 1 sec averaging time. The chip is fabricated using the Advanced Micro Foundry standard silicon photonic process and occupies a footprint of 10 mm^2.
tldr: The authors demonstrate an electro-optic self-injection-locking silicon photonic chip that stabilizes a commercial DFB diode laser to a 58 mHz fundamental linewidth using a co-integrated high-Q vacuum-gap micro-Fabry-Perot cavity.
motivation: Compact, chip-scale ultra-stable lasers are needed for portable optical clocks, precision metrology, and coherent communication, but conventional stabilization systems rely on bulky tabletop optics and complex locking electronics.
method: A silicon photonic chip integrating an electro-optic self-injection-locking (EOSIL) loop with a modulation-free frequency stabilization scheme and a vacuum-gap micro-cavity (Q ≈ 3.46×10^9) is fabricated on a standard AMF silicon photonics process in a 10 mm^2 footprint.
result: The chip suppresses the DFB laser's frequency noise by more than 110 dB at 1 Hz offset, reaching a fundamental linewidth of 58 mHz and fractional frequency instability of 8.68×10^-13 at 1 s, close to the cavity thermal-noise limit.
conclusion: The work shows that wafer-scale silicon photonics can deliver sub-Hz-linewidth laser stabilization in a compact package, enabling fieldable precision metrology and serving as a potential building block for integrated quantum-photonic and optical-clock platforms.

title: Development Of A Fabrication-to-benchtop Process For SiN-based Quantum Devices
authors: Connor Kupchak, Abubaker Tareki, Tara Moradi, Patrick Laferriere, Niall Tait, Khaled Mnaymneh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Silicon nitride has emerged as a key material for the advancement of future quantum communication and computational devices. However, challenges persist in establishing a comprehensive development process, spanning from fabrication to optical characterization, essential for advancing these devices to their next stage of potential. Maintaining control over the entire process, from start to finish, alongside device modeling, enables more efficient and timely iteration and optimization. Here we introduce a fabrication-to-benchtop process. We employ an in-house stoichiometric recipe for device fabrication and conduct comprehensive characterization of optical losses and material properties. Understanding and controlling the refractive index of the device are vital for predicting device geometries and group indices. Implementing the refractive indices of our fabricated devices, we simulate microring resonators and demonstrate their application in generating optical solitons.
tldr: The paper presents a fabrication-to-benchtop workflow for silicon nitride photonic devices, including optical loss characterization and microring resonator simulations.
motivation: Silicon nitride is a promising material for quantum communication and computation devices, but an integrated process from fabrication to optical characterization is needed to enable rapid iteration and optimization.
method: The authors develop an in-house stoichiometric fabrication recipe, characterize optical losses and material properties, extract refractive indices, and use these to simulate microring resonators for soliton generation.
result: The process yields devices with characterized optical losses and material properties, and simulations show that the fabricated refractive indices support microring resonators capable of generating optical solitons.
conclusion: A controlled fabrication-to-benchtop pipeline can support the development of SiN-based quantum photonic devices, though the work focuses on classical optical characterization rather than quantum information protocols.

title: Noise Correlation Spectroscopy: A Review
authors: Gombojav O. Ariunbold
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22392v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The frequency noise of an ordinary diode laser, often a nuisance in spectroscopy, can be used to measure atomic coherence. When atoms are prepared in a coherent superposition of two ground states, each random shift in laser frequency changes how much light they absorb, so the transmitted light carries a record of that coherence. Correlating the intensity fluctuations of two fields, each linking one ground state to a shared excited state, reads this record out, a technique known as noise correlation spectroscopy. The correlation signal is narrower than the transparency window the same fields create and switches sign as their frequency difference is tuned. Its width is set by the rate at which the atoms lose coherence and, over a wide range, does not grow with laser power. Over two decades the method has spread from warm vapors to cold atoms, to multi-field schemes, and to diamond and rare-earth-doped crystals. This review, to the author's knowledge the first, brings together its theory, experiments and applications, and examines its limits, the challenges that remain, and the opportunities that could make it a standard spectroscopic tool.
tldr: This review surveys noise correlation spectroscopy, a technique that uses laser frequency-noise correlations to read out atomic coherence in vapors, cold atoms, diamond, and rare-earth-doped crystals.
motivation: Laser frequency noise is usually unwanted in spectroscopy, but it can serve as a probe of atomic coherence when atoms are in a superposition of ground states.
method: The paper reviews theory and experiments in which intensity fluctuations of two optical fields are correlated to extract a narrow signal whose width reflects the atomic decoherence rate.
result: The correlation signal is narrower than the associated transparency window, changes sign with two-photon detuning, and is largely independent of laser power over a wide range.
conclusion: The review collects two decades of developments and discusses remaining challenges and opportunities for making noise correlation spectroscopy a standard tool.

title: Physics-Transfer Learning: A Physics-Constrained Theory For Zero-Shot Generalization Along The Ladder Of Complexity
authors: Zhiping Xu Yingjie Zhao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reliable out-of-distribution generalization remains a central challenge in machine learning, particularly when models are deployed in data-scarce high-fidelity domains. Existing approaches often rely on statistical distribution alignment, or invariance assumptions that can fail when domain shifts reflect changes in underlying mechanisms. Inspired by a longstanding paradigm in physics that understands complex systems by starting from tractable idealizations and progressively incorporating additional mechanisms and levels of fidelity, we propose physics-transfer (PT) learning, a physics-constrained learning theory for zero-shot generalization along a ladder of complexity. PT constructs chains of anchor domains (CADs) that connect low-cost source domains to complex targets and introduces computable feasibility and reliability indicators for assessing transfer before target-domain labels are observed. Under physical-consistency and stable-representation assumptions, we derive an operational upper bound on target risk in terms of source empirical risk, the PT indicators, and finite-sample errors, and establish convergence as adjacent complexity gaps shrink and data coverage improves. We evaluate PT on excited-state energy prediction in quantum systems and dynamical-transition prediction in classical systems using neural networks trained without target-domain labels. Across substantial distribution shifts, PT yields accurate high-fidelity predictions, while the indicators identify incorrect physical mappings before target-domain prediction fails. These results provide a model-agnostic framework for designing, diagnosing, and controlling generalization in data-scarce learning problems.
tldr: The paper proposes physics-transfer learning, a physics-constrained framework for zero-shot generalization across domains of increasing complexity, with applications to quantum excited-state energies and classical dynamics.
motivation: Out-of-distribution generalization is difficult when high-fidelity target data are scarce and distribution shifts arise from changes in underlying physical mechanisms rather than simple statistical differences.
method: The authors construct chains of anchor domains connecting low-cost source domains to complex targets and derive computable feasibility/reliability indicators plus an operational target-risk upper bound under physical-consistency and stable-representation assumptions.
result: Neural networks trained without target-domain labels achieve accurate high-fidelity predictions under substantial distribution shifts, and the proposed indicators can detect incorrect physical mappings before prediction failure.
conclusion: Physics-transfer learning offers a model-agnostic framework for designing and diagnosing generalization in data-scarce scientific machine learning, though it is not centered on quantum information theory or related research directions.

title: SemQBench: Benchmarking Decomposition-Aware Runtime Policies For Quantum-HPC Search
authors: Yogesh Simmhan Chandrachud Pati
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22886v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum processors are increasingly used as accelerators inside high-performance computing (HPC) workflows. A workflow runtime decides which quantum circuits to run, how to group them into provider jobs, and what to repeat after a failed attempt. Many search problems split into independent parts, but the runtime can use that structure only when the workflow exposes the parts and a validity check for each one. SemQBench measures what a runtime gains from this visibility. It compares seven execution policies for the same search problem, including two controls without amplitude amplification. The policies change one runtime choice at a time: whether to amplify, whether partial results may be combined across runs, whether the parts share one circuit, and what a retry keeps. We run them on the 20-qubit IQM Garnet processor using 106 distinct circuits in three jobs, and report circuit executions, active device time, and provider jobs separately before combining them in a cost model. Amplifying the problem as one whole circuit shows no statistically clear gain over random sampling and uses 6.7-104[MATH] more active device time. Exposing the parts and collecting valid partial results across a fixed batch of runs cuts the executions needed for 95% completion confidence by 2.20-4.00[MATH], and this policy is never worse than the other amplified policies in executions, device time, or jobs; it is selected in 99 of 108 overhead settings. Fewer executions do not always mean less device time: on one workload, executions fall from thirteen to four while active device time rises from 7.44 to 9.81 [MATH]s. Exposing problem structure therefore gives the runtime a strong default policy and the measurements needed to decide when the simpler unamplified option is cheaper.
tldr: SemQBench benchmarks seven runtime execution policies for quantum-HPC search workflows on a 20-qubit IQM Garnet device, showing that exposing problem structure and combining valid partial results outperforms whole-problem amplitude amplification.
motivation: Quantum processors used as accelerators in HPC workflows require runtime decisions about circuit grouping, amplification, partial-result combination, and retry strategy, but the benefit of exposing decomposable problem structure had not been quantified empirically.
method: The authors define seven execution policies differing in one runtime choice at a time (amplification, partial-result combination, shared circuit, retry semantics), run them with 106 distinct circuits across three jobs on IQM Garnet, and compare circuit executions, active device time, and provider jobs separately and under a combined cost model.
result: Whole-problem amplification yields no statistically clear gain over random sampling while consuming 6.7–104x more device time; the structure-exposing partial-result policy reduces executions for 95% completion confidence by 2.20–4.00x, is never worse across metrics, and is selected in 99 of 108 overhead settings, though reduced executions can sometimes increase device time.
conclusion: Exposing decomposition structure gives workflow runtimes a strong default policy, and the reported measurements enable deciding when the simpler unamplified option is cheaper.

title: Trapping Of Nanofabricated SiO$_2$ High-aspect-ratio Discs In An Optical Lattice
authors: Shelby Klomp, Shafaq Gulzar Elahi, Scott Grudichak, Chethn Galla, Zhiyuan Wang, Mark Nguyen, George Winstone, Katarina Boskovic Guy, Emma Derrick, Maddox Wroblewski, Jacob Sprague, Andrew Laeuger, Jackson Larsen, Nancy Aggarwal, Shane L. Larson, Andrew A. Geraci
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22614v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We describe the nanofabrication and loading of lithographically patterned, high aspect ratio [MATH] [MATH]m diameter silicon dioxide discs with thickness of [MATH] nm into an optical standing wave trap in vacuum. We obtain motional spectra of the center of mass motion of the discs using a combination of interferometric and imaging methods. The method is capable of high-efficiency loading and optical trapping using small numbers of objects, of the order of a few particles, with customized geometries and sizes compatible with wafer scale nanofabrication methods. Disc-like particles in optical traps have been identified as promising candidates for detectors of high frequency gravitational waves or as sensitive accelerometers.
tldr: The paper demonstrates nanofabrication and optical trapping of high-aspect-ratio SiO2 discs in a standing-wave optical lattice in vacuum, with motional spectra measured interferometrically and by imaging.
motivation: Disc-shaped levitated particles are proposed as sensitive detectors for high-frequency gravitational waves and accelerometers, motivating efficient trapping and characterization of custom nanofabricated objects.
method: Lithographically patterned SiO2 discs with micrometer-scale diameters and nanometer thicknesses are loaded into an optical standing wave in vacuum; center-of-mass motion is measured using interferometric and imaging techniques.
result: The authors achieve high-efficiency loading and trapping of a few particles with customized geometries and sizes, obtaining motional spectra compatible with wafer-scale nanofabrication.
conclusion: The platform is promising for high-frequency gravitational-wave detection and accelerometry, though it does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid qubit systems.

title: Quantum Approximate Stochastic Combinatorial Optimisation
authors: Edric Matwiejew, Paulo E. Santos, Jingbo B. Wang, Ugo Varetto
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two-stage stochastic combinatorial optimisation concerns discrete decisions made before all relevant information is known. An initial decision is made; once uncertainty is resolved, it can be adapted to the realised scenario, at a cost. The aim is to find the initial decision that minimises the upfront cost plus the expected cost of optimal adaptation. The first-stage decision problem is often NP-hard, and computing the expected minimum recourse cost can be [MATH]-hard for a single first-stage candidate. We introduce Quantum Approximate Stochastic Combinatorial Optimisation (QASCO), a variational quantum-walk ansatz that coherently incorporates scenario-dependent recourse into its dynamics to search over first-stage decisions without explicitly evaluating expected minimum recourse costs. We demonstrate QASCO for MaxCut with stochastic edge weights, obtain a circuit with polynomial per-layer gate complexity, and study the ansatz via exact state-vector simulation. Across the instances considered, QASCO concentrates amplitude more effectively on stochastic-optimal first-stage decisions than a previously proposed two-stage QAOA construction. We further show that the ansatz can be calibrated using a depth-independent number of parameters and applied to unseen instances without further circuit-parameter optimisation, including joint decision--scenario--recourse spaces spanning more than [MATH] configurations. Under a query-cost model, comparison with the tested classical heuristics using sample-average approximations of the expected minimum recourse cost shows that QASCO more reliably reaches globally optimal first-stage solutions while requiring fewer cut evaluations. These results show how to incorporate scenario-dependent recourse into the ansatz dynamics, providing a general framework for variational quantum walks in two-stage stochastic combinatorial optimisation.
tldr: The paper introduces QASCO, a variational quantum-walk ansatz that embeds scenario-dependent recourse directly into the circuit dynamics to solve two-stage stochastic combinatorial optimisation problems such as MaxCut with stochastic edge weights.
motivation: Two-stage stochastic optimisation requires evaluating expected minimum recourse costs, which is #P-hard per first-stage candidate and NP-hard overall, making classical sample-average approaches expensive and unreliable.
method: The authors construct a polynomial-depth variational quantum-walk ansatz whose dynamics coherently incorporate recourse across scenarios, and benchmark it via exact state-vector simulation against a prior two-stage QAOA construction and classical heuristics.
result: QASCO concentrates amplitude more effectively on stochastic-optimal first-stage decisions, can be calibrated with a depth-independent parameter count, transfers to unseen instances without re-optimisation, and reaches global optima with fewer cut evaluations under a query-cost model.
conclusion: The work provides a general framework for embedding scenario-dependent recourse in variational quantum walks, offering a NISQ-compatible heuristic for stochastic combinatorial optimisation.

title: Diffusion-controlled Reactions With Time-dependent Surface Reactivity
authors: Yilin Ye Denis S. Grebenkov
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate diffusion-controlled reactions on a reactive surface with time-dependent reactivity. Starting from a conventional formulation via diffusion equation with Robin boundary condition for the macroscopic concentration of particles, we aim at quantifying how temporal variations of reactivity affect the survival probability and the associated first-reaction time (FRT) of a single particle on the reactive surface. Using an adiabatic description, we first identify five long-time regimes of the first-reaction time distribution, ranging from exponential and stretched-exponential to power-law decay. In particular, sufficiently rapid decay of the reactivity leads to a nonzero probability of never reacting, despite diffusion in a bounded domain. Second, we provide a probabilistic reformulation of this problem and compare it with a different scenario of encounter-dependent reactivity. Our theoretical predictions are validated via extensive Monte Carlo simulations.
tldr: The authors analyze diffusion-controlled reactions on a reactive surface whose reactivity decays in time, classifying long-time regimes of the first-reaction-time distribution and showing that rapid reactivity decay can yield a nonzero probability of never reacting even in a bounded domain.
motivation: Surface reactivity in real catalytic and biological systems fluctuates in time, yet most diffusion-controlled reaction theory assumes constant reactivity; the paper aims to quantify how temporal variation of reactivity alters survival probability and first-reaction times.
method: Starting from the diffusion equation with a time-dependent Robin boundary condition, the authors use an adiabatic description to derive long-time asymptotics of the first-reaction time distribution, then give a probabilistic reformulation and compare with an encounter-dependent reactivity scenario, validating predictions by extensive Monte Carlo simulations.
result: Five long-time regimes are identified — exponential, stretched-exponential, and power-law decays among them — and sufficiently fast decay of the reactivity produces a strictly positive survival probability at infinite time despite bounded-domain diffusion.
conclusion: Time-dependent surface reactivity qualitatively enriches the phenomenology of diffusion-controlled reactions, breaking the standard certainty of eventual reaction and providing a tractable adiabatic framework testable against simulation.

title: Wavelength Diversity Expands The Expressive Power Of Optical Computing
authors: Shiqi Chen, Che-Yung Shen, Parnian Ghapandar Kashani, Yongkang Cheng, Aydogan Ozcan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23070v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Universal function approximation underpins neural networks' capacity to represent nonlinear relationships, but realizing this capability in optical hardware requires engineering the computational features encoded in light. Here, we show that wavelength diversity enhances optical function-approximation expressivity through wavelength-scaled Fourier features generated by a shared phase encoder, without increasing the number of input-encoded harmonics. Multiple wavelengths contribute to the representation of each output function rather than merely serving as independent computational channels. We establish theoretical scaling laws and approximation-error bounds, revealing that, for nondispersive encoders, the spectral endpoints determine the accessible computational bandwidth, while intermediate illumination wavelengths enrich the available harmonics within that bandwidth. Numerical studies demonstrate improved approximation of real- and complex-valued nonlinear functions, with a representative design achieving more than a 100-fold reduction in mean-squared error relative to tested monochromatic optical processors with the same number of trainable phase features. Experimentally, we validate enhanced approximation accuracy and demonstrate the simultaneous approximation of 4,136 distinct nonlinear functions using a compact, single-layer diffractive processor under five-wavelength illumination. These results establish wavelength diversity as an additional physical resource for scaling the expressive power of optical computing and enhancing the accuracy of parallel nonlinear function approximation.
tldr: Wavelength diversity in a shared phase-encoded diffractive optical processor is shown to increase the expressive power of optical function approximation, with theory, numerics, and a five-wavelength experiment demonstrating large accuracy gains.
motivation: Optical neural hardware needs a way to represent rich nonlinear functions, and the authors ask whether using multiple illumination wavelengths — rather than a single monochromatic channel — can expand the set of accessible computational features.
method: They derive scaling laws and approximation-error bounds for wavelength-scaled Fourier features produced by a nondispersive shared phase encoder, then validate with numerical benchmarks and a compact single-layer diffractive processor under five-wavelength illumination approximating 4,136 distinct nonlinear functions.
result: The analysis shows spectral endpoints set the accessible computational bandwidth while intermediate wavelengths enrich the harmonics within it, yielding over 100-fold MSE reduction versus monochromatic processors with the same number of trainable phase features, and experimental confirmation of enhanced accuracy and massively parallel function approximation.
conclusion: Wavelength diversity is proposed as an additional physical resource for scaling expressive power in optical computing and improving parallel nonlinear function approximation.

title: Thermodynamics Of Coupled Electromagnetic And Mass Fields
authors: Fei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We formulate a unified thermodynamic framework for chemical, mechanical, and electromagnetic transport by extending the Gibbs--Duhem relation to include kinetic free-energy contributions associated with material and field motion. The resulting kinetic Gibbs--Duhem relation establishes a thermodynamic connection between free-energy variations, generalized chemical potentials, pressure, and transport momentum, while preserving the invariance of the system free energy under changes of reference frame. Within a Lagrangian formulation of free-energy evolution, the relation provides a common structure for diffusion, momentum transport, and electromagnetic dynamics. For nonuniform chemical systems, the framework recovers the coupling between Cahn--Hilliard dynamics and the Korteweg stress arising from composition gradients. Its extension to electromagnetic systems incorporates electric, magnetic, charge, and mechanical contributions into the same thermodynamic formulation, yielding a unified description of electromagnetic and momentum evolution. The framework further separates dissipative from nondissipative transport and establishes a common thermodynamic form for mechanical and electromagnetic propagation. In the isentropic limit, the characteristic propagation velocity is determined by the derivative of the thermodynamic pressure with respect to density, yielding the speed of sound for mechanical systems and the speed of light for electromagnetic systems. These results show that kinetic contributions can be incorporated consistently into the Gibbs--Duhem framework, providing a common thermodynamic basis for coupled chemical, mechanical, and electromagnetic transport without introducing separate thermodynamic principles for each mechanism.
tldr: The paper extends the Gibbs--Duhem relation to include kinetic contributions and formulates a unified classical thermodynamic framework for coupled chemical, mechanical, and electromagnetic transport.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a common thermodynamic basis for diffusion, momentum transport, and electromagnetic dynamics without introducing separate principles for each transport mechanism.
method: They derive a kinetic Gibbs--Duhem relation within a Lagrangian free-energy formulation, recovering Cahn--Hilliard dynamics with Korteweg stress and incorporating electric, magnetic, charge, and mechanical contributions.
result: The framework separates dissipative from nondissipative transport and shows that in the isentropic limit the propagation speed follows from the derivative of pressure with respect to density, yielding sound speed for mechanical systems and light speed for electromagnetic systems.
conclusion: Kinetic contributions can be consistently included in the Gibbs--Duhem framework, offering a unified classical thermodynamic description of coupled transport phenomena.

title: Advanced Computational Methods For Simulating The Classical Hydrogen Atom In Stochastic Electrodynamics
authors: Daniel C. Cole
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stochastic electrodynamics (SED) is a theory of nature that seeks to derive key aspects of quantum mechanics and quantum electrodynamics from a purely classical physics perspective. While SED has been successful in many areas, it has largely failed to stably simulate the 3D classical hydrogen atom. The computational methodology presented here overcomes these foundational challenges. We develop a pseudo-wave formulation that integrates the solid angle in k-space utilizing symmetry, resulting in a significantly reduced memory footprint and lower computational overhead for generating the zero-point radiation spectrum. This optimization is paired with a logarithmic frequency grid, a sliding window tracking the instantaneous Keplerian frequency, and a Tukey smoothing function to eliminate discrete force discontinuities. Integrated via an adaptive RKF45 solver across highly dense grids of up to 100-million bins, these techniques demonstrate the asymptotic convergence of ensemble stability. We show that increasing the grid resolution in the high-frequency domain systematically mitigates artificial electron decay, yielding a simulated probability density function that closely aligns with the quantum mechanical ground state P(r).
tldr: The paper presents optimized computational methods for simulating the classical hydrogen atom in stochastic electrodynamics, aiming to reproduce quantum ground-state behavior from a classical framework.
motivation: Stochastic electrodynamics seeks to derive quantum phenomena from classical physics, but prior simulations of the 3D hydrogen atom suffered from numerical instabilities and artificial electron decay.
method: The authors develop a pseudo-wave formulation that integrates solid angle in k-space, uses a logarithmic frequency grid, sliding-window Keplerian frequency tracking, Tukey smoothing, and an adaptive RKF45 solver over dense spectral grids.
result: Higher grid resolution in the high-frequency domain mitigates artificial decay, and the simulated probability density converges toward the quantum mechanical ground-state radial distribution P(r).
conclusion: The proposed computational techniques enable stable ensemble simulations of the classical hydrogen atom in SED, supporting the program of recovering quantum behavior from a classical stochastic framework.

title: A Configurational Numerical Viscosity For Thermodynamically Compatible Finite Volume Schemes Of Compressible Multiphase Flows
authors: Davide Ferrari, Ilya Peshkov, Michael Dumbser
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23247v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the fluid subsystem of a variationally derived hyperbolic thermodynamically compatible (HTC) model of compressible multiphase flows. Its total energy is in general not convex in the natural state variables, so a scalar numerical viscosity acting on them need not produce non-negative entropy. Reformulating the equations in terms of the volume fractions separates changes in the amount of each phase from changes in its intrinsic state. This guides the construction of a configurational numerical viscosity in phase variables, in which the energy is convex, while the scheme retains the structure of the HTC model. At the semi-discrete level, the new schemes satisfy: I) local conservation of the phase masses, the mixture momentum and the total energy; II) a cell entropy inequality whose production is non-negative face by face and phase by phase, with no convexity assumption in the evolved variables and no clipping; III) positivity of the partial densities and volume fractions under explicit time-step conditions; IV) exact preservation of contact equilibria; V) equivalence with a scheme for the density-weighted volume fractions. The key ingredients are: i) an exact decomposition of the jump of each phase across a face into a configurational part, dissipated with the material speed, and an intrinsic part, dissipated with the acoustic speed; ii) an exchange form of this dissipation between neighbouring cells, with non-negative weights; iii) a side-wise transfer of the dissipation to the evolved variables through the chain rule of each cell, which turns the energy defects into Bregman divergences of the single-fluid energies; iv) a thermodynamic correction of the reversible part built in the phase variables. Properties I)-V) are proved and verified numerically, including a shock tube in which the Rusanov viscosity produces negative entropy and a shock-water column interaction.
tldr: The authors construct a configurational numerical viscosity for finite-volume discretizations of compressible multiphase flow models that are thermodynamically compatible, ensuring non-negative entropy production without convexity assumptions.
motivation: In variationally derived hyperbolic thermodynamically compatible (HTC) models of multiphase flow, the total energy is not convex in the natural state variables, so standard scalar numerical viscosities can generate negative entropy and break positivity or contact preservation.
method: Reformulating the system in volume-fraction (phase) variables makes the energy convex; jumps across faces are split into configurational parts dissipated at material speed and intrinsic parts dissipated at acoustic speed, with an exchange-form dissipation and a thermodynamic correction of the reversible flux.
result: The semi-discrete schemes provably conserve phase masses, mixture momentum and total energy; satisfy a cell entropy inequality with face-by-face, phase-by-phase non-negative production without clipping; preserve positivity of densities and volume fractions, keep contact equilibria exact, and remain equivalent to a density-weighted volume-fraction scheme, verified on shock-tube and shock–water-column tests.
conclusion: Structural reformulation in phase variables yields robust entropy-stable finite-volume schemes for non-convex HTC multiphase models, though the contribution is purely classical computational fluid dynamics.

title: Nonrelativistic Quantum Theory Of Non-dipole Effects In A Multielectron Atom: Radiation Transition Operator
authors: Alexey N. Hopersky, Alexey M. Nadolinsky, Rustam V. Koneev
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22527v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the work of Hopersky A.N. et al., arXiv: 2609.33494v1 [physics. atom-ph] in the Loudon integral representation, the general analytical structure of the complete operator of a multipole radiation transition taking into account non-dipole effects for a multielectron atom is established. In this Letter this structure is converted to the sum only for all multipoles.
tldr: This letter derives a multipole-sum representation of the radiation transition operator for non-dipole effects in multielectron atoms.
motivation: The authors aim to simplify the general analytical structure of the complete multipole radiation-transition operator established in prior work using the Loudon integral representation.
method: The previously derived general operator accounting for non-dipole effects in a multielectron atom is converted into a sum over all multipoles.
result: The complete radiation-transition operator is expressed as a sum solely over all multipoles, providing a simplified analytical form.
conclusion: The result offers a more compact operator representation for describing non-dipole radiative transitions in multielectron atoms, though it lies outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid quantum systems.

title: Metric And Dispersive Dynamics Of Phase Perturbations In Bohmian Quantum Mechanics
authors: Hermano Velten Felipe S. Esc\'orcio
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: By linearizing the hydrodynamic equations associated with the Madelung transformation in the context of Bohmian dynamics, we derive an effective metric for the phase perturbation around a background state. We show that the metric previously obtained previously by the same authors arises naturally as a particular case of a more general structure, in which the complete functional variation of the quantum potential is retained and external classical potentials can be incorporated. This generalization preserves the dependence of the quantum potential on the density and its spatial derivatives, generating additional terms that introduce dispersive corrections and act as sources in the effective Klein-Gordon equation. To organize these contributions, we introduce differential operators that separate the local sector responsible for the effective geometry from the corrections associated with the complete functional structure of the quantum potential. We identify the conditions under which these additional terms become negligible, recovering homogeneous propagation and the effective geometry for the Gaussian wave packet of a free particle.
tldr: The paper derives an effective metric and dispersive corrections for phase perturbations in Bohmian quantum mechanics by linearizing the Madelung hydrodynamic equations with the full functional variation of the quantum potential.
motivation: The authors aim to generalize their previous effective metric for phase perturbations around a background state in Bohmian dynamics and to incorporate external classical potentials and dispersive corrections from the quantum potential.
method: They linearize the hydrodynamic equations associated with the Madelung transformation, retain the complete functional variation of the quantum potential, introduce differential operators to separate local geometric terms from dispersive source terms, and derive an effective Klein-Gordon equation.
result: The earlier metric emerges as a special case of a more general structure; additional terms introduce dispersive corrections and act as sources, and conditions are identified under which these terms become negligible, recovering homogeneous propagation for a free Gaussian wave packet.
conclusion: The work provides a generalized geometric description of phase perturbations in Bohmian quantum mechanics, but it is focused on quantum foundations and hydrodynamic analogies rather than the user's quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems interests.

title: An Improved Limit On $^{171}\text{Yb}$ Electric Dipole Moment
authors: S. -Z. Wang, S. -B. Wang, E. F. Zhou, Z. -J. Tao, J. -M. Yao, T. Xia, Z. -T. Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Searches for permanent electric dipole moments (EDMs) probe new sources of CP violation beyond the Standard Model. The atomic EDM of [MATH], which is sensitive to its nuclear Schiff moment, is a promising candidate, but previous measurements were limited by noise and systematic effects induced by the optical dipole trap (ODT) that holds the atoms. Here we report a substantially improved search enabled by a dual-ODT configuration with orthogonal polarizations, and spin measurements for precise alignment of static and optical fields. By suppressing the key parity-mixing systematic effect and vector light-shift noise, we achieve a limit of [MATH] (95\% C.L.), which represents a 20-fold improvement over the previous work. We also present the first calculation of the nuclear structure factors of the Schiff moment of [MATH]. The experimental and theoretical advances combine to tighten constraints on CP-violating pion-nucleon couplings in a global analysis. Moreover, this work demonstrates a pathway toward future measurements in [MATH], where nuclear deformation offers exceptional sensitivity to physics beyond the Standard Model.
tldr: An improved atomic electric dipole moment search in 171Yb using a dual optical dipole trap configuration, achieving a 20-fold improvement in the EDM limit and tighter constraints on CP-violating pion-nucleon couplings.
motivation: Permanent EDMs probe new sources of CP violation beyond the Standard Model, but prior 171Yb measurements were limited by noise and systematic effects induced by the single optical dipole trap used to hold the atoms.
method: A dual-ODT configuration with orthogonal polarizations plus spin measurements for precise alignment of static and optical fields suppresses parity-mixing systematics and vector light-shift noise; the authors also perform the first calculation of nuclear structure factors of the 171Yb Schiff moment.
result: A limit of ~10^-30 e·cm scale (95% C.L.) is obtained, a 20-fold improvement over previous work, and global analysis tightens constraints on CP-violating pion-nucleon couplings.
conclusion: The work establishes a pathway toward future EDM measurements in deformed nuclei with exceptional sensitivity to beyond-Standard-Model physics, but is an atomic precision-metrology experiment with no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Asymptotic Evaluation Of Multidimensional Oscillatory Integrals
authors: Job Feldbrugge Samuel Crew
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22767v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Oscillatory integrals appear throughout physics, from diffraction and gravitational lensing to real-time path integrals. Their asymptotic evaluation is complicated by the need to determine which real and complex saddle points contribute, and how they are connected by Stokes phenomena. In multiple dimensions, this traditionally requires computing steepest descent manifolds in a high-dimensional complex space. Here, we develop an algebraic alternative for integrals with polynomial and rational exponents. Using integration by parts and Brieskorn reduction, we construct a finite-dimensional Gauss-Manin system that generates the asymptotic expansion of all saddle points. Its Borel transform yields a Fuchsian system, whose mondromy determines the Stokes constants and hence the adjacency of the saddle points. Combined with the recent South-East rule, this identifies the contributing saddles and enables superasymptotic and hyperasymptotic approximations without computing gradient flows. We demonstate the method for the parabolic umbilic diffraction integral and a Lorentzian lens as examples, obtaining agreement to machine precision. The methods are implemented in an accompanying open-source Julia package Resurgence.jl.
tldr: The paper develops an algebraic method based on Gauss-Manin systems and Brieskorn reduction to asymptotically evaluate multidimensional oscillatory integrals without explicitly computing steepest-descent manifolds.
motivation: Oscillatory integrals arise across physics, but their multidimensional asymptotic evaluation is complicated by identifying contributing real and complex saddle points and tracking Stokes phenomena.
method: Using integration by parts and Brieskorn reduction, the authors construct a finite-dimensional Gauss-Manin system whose Borel transform gives a Fuchsian system; its monodromy determines Stokes constants and saddle-point adjacency, which together with the South-East rule identifies contributing saddles.
result: The method is demonstrated on the parabolic umbilic diffraction integral and a Lorentzian lens, achieving agreement to machine precision and enabling superasymptotic and hyperasymptotic approximations.
conclusion: This provides a practical algebraic alternative to gradient-flow computations for multidimensional oscillatory integrals, implemented in the open-source Julia package Resurgence.jl.

title: Fully Relativistic Calculation Of Thermal Shifts In Spectra Of Hydrogen Molecular Ion
authors: M. A. Reiter, A. A. Anikin, A. A. Kotov, D. A. Glazov, T. A. Zalialiutdinov, D. A. Solovyev
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Within a fully relativistic framework, we discuss the one-loop self-energy correction, generalized to the presence of external blackbody radiation, for a bound electron in the hydrogen molecular ion. The calculations rely on the thermal part of the photon propagator from finite-temperature quantum electrodynamics. The Dirac equation with a two-center potential is solved using the dual kinetic balance condition, extended to axially symmetric systems, and a B-spline-based trial function. The results are obtained within the Born-Oppenheimer adiabatic approximation. Thermal shift for the ground term of the hydrogen molecular ion is computed as a function of the internuclear distance. Including this correction, we present the resulting shifts of the vibrational levels. The analysis focuses on the dynamical effect, a comparison is made with data available in the current literature.
tldr: The paper computes fully relativistic finite-temperature QED corrections to thermal shifts in the hydrogen molecular ion spectra.
motivation: Thermal blackbody-radiation shifts are important for high-precision spectroscopy of molecular ions, but fully relativistic treatments are needed for accurate level predictions.
method: The authors evaluate the one-loop self-energy correction in the presence of blackbody radiation using the thermal photon propagator from finite-temperature QED, solving the two-center Dirac equation with dual kinetic balance and B-spline basis functions in the Born-Oppenheimer approximation.
result: Thermal shifts of the ground term are calculated as a function of internuclear distance, and the corresponding shifts of vibrational levels are presented and compared with existing literature.
conclusion: The work provides relativistic finite-temperature QED predictions for thermal spectral shifts in H2+, relevant to precision molecular spectroscopy rather than quantum information science.

title: Parity-dependent Sublattice Structure Of Local $2\times2$ Correlations In Domino Tilings Of The Aztec Diamond
authors: Chaeyeon Kim, Suhwan Yoo, Jeehoon Choi, Hee Young Kwon, Changyeon Won
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22974v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study local [MATH] correlations in uniformly random domino tilings of the Aztec diamond [MATH], a dimer model with frozen corners and a liquid region bounded by the Arctic circle, and compare them with the square chessboard. For every elementary square the probabilities [MATH] and [MATH] of the two coverings by a pair of parallel dominoes satisfy [MATH], where [MATH] are the probabilities of the four surrounding edges. This known identity, a case of Kuo's graphical condensation, reduces the spatial profile of [MATH] to single-edge probabilities, which we compute exactly from the inverse Kasteleyn matrix for all squares of [MATH]. The squares form two interleaved sublattices, distinguished by the color of their lower-left cell. The parity of [MATH] decides which sublattice dominates near the center: the one containing the central square for odd [MATH], and the other one for even [MATH]. This sign rule holds for the averaged sublattice contrast for all [MATH]. It also fixes the location of the global maximum of [MATH], which lies at or next to the center for odd [MATH] and several lattice spacings away for even [MATH]. Within the central sublattice, the preferred square follows a mod-4 pattern that matches the exactly pinned mean height of the center. On the [MATH] chessboard the same rule holds with [MATH] replaced by the half-width [MATH], but the contrast is two to six times weaker, the central edge probability never equals [MATH], and the maxima of [MATH] are pinned to the corners. The exact [MATH] values and the interior, parity-selected maxima are therefore features of the Aztec geometry.
tldr: An exact combinatorial study of local 2x2 domino-pair correlations in uniformly random tilings of the Aztec diamond, showing a parity-dependent sublattice structure of the Arctic-circle liquid region.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize the spatial profile of local 2x2 correlations in Aztec diamond dimer models and contrast it with the square chessboard lattice, exploiting Kuo's graphical condensation to reduce these to single-edge probabilities.
method: Using Kuo's condensation identity, the probability of parallel domino pairs in each elementary square is expressed via the four surrounding edge probabilities, which are computed exactly from the inverse Kasteleyn matrix for all squares of the diamond.
result: The squares split into two interleaved sublattices whose relative dominance is set by the parity of the diamond size, fixing the location of the global maximum of the correlation and producing a mod-4 pattern tied to the pinned mean height; the chessboard shows a much weaker analogue with corner-pinned maxima.
conclusion: The exact correlation values and interior, parity-selected maxima are specific features of the Aztec diamond geometry rather than generic lattice properties.

title: Quantum Periods From Tba And Continued Fractions
authors: Alexander Chervov, Ilia Gaiur, Sergey Galkin, Fedor Levkovich-Maslyuk, Volodya Rubtsov, Shamil Shakirov
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider quantum A-periods of local [MATH], or equivalently the generating function of constant terms for powers of the Laurent polynomial [MATH] where [MATH] and [MATH] are [MATH]-commuting variables. We derive a number of new representations for these rich combinatorial and algebraic objects. First, we find that the well-known TBA equation encodes not only the A-period itself but also higher diagonal modes of the corresponding noncommutative Laurent polynomials. Second, we obtain new formulas for the period in terms of continued fractions and related orthogonal polynomials, as well as a nontrivial explicit recursion allowing its efficient computation. Finally, we compute quantum corrections to the classical Picard-Fuchs equation, and observe that holonomicity of the classical period does not generalise to [MATH]-holonomicity of its quantum counterpart. Applications to random walks on the Cayley graph of the Heisenberg group, and related new approaches to more efficient generative AI systems, are outlined.
tldr: The paper studies quantum A-periods via TBA equations, continued fractions, orthogonal polynomials, and q-deformed Picard-Fuchs structures.
motivation: It aims to uncover new algebraic and combinatorial representations of quantum periods arising from noncommutative Laurent polynomials and q-commuting variables.
method: The authors use thermodynamic Bethe ansatz equations, continued-fraction expansions, orthogonal polynomial techniques, explicit recursions, and quantum corrections to Picard-Fuchs equations.
result: They show TBA encodes higher diagonal modes, derive new period formulas and efficient recursions, and find that classical holonomicity does not straightforwardly extend to q-holonomicity.
conclusion: The work develops mathematical structures around quantum periods with possible applications to Heisenberg-group random walks and generative AI, but it is not directly aligned with quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Universal Operators: Topology And Consequences Of Isp Failure
authors: Jo\~ao Carmo, Ben-Hur Eidt, Waleed Noor
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Assuming a negative answer to the invariant subspace problem for separable complex Hilbert spaces, we prove that every universal operator has a continuum of minimal infinite-dimensional invariant subspaces with pairwise trivial intersections. These subspaces can be chosen so that the restrictions are invertible and their powers decay at any prescribed geometric rate. For an affine composition operator on the Hardy space \(H^2(\D)\), we derive restrictions on the zeros, inner factors and Hardy regularity of generators, and construct minimal models with radial vanishing of any prescribed finite order. Independently of the invariant subspace problem, we identify the norm interior, closure and boundary of the universal operator class. Its interior is the Caradus--Pozzi class, its closure is the complement of the upper semi-Fredholm class, and its boundary consists of the operators that are neither upper nor lower semi-Fredholm.
tldr: A pure functional-analysis paper on universal operators and the invariant subspace problem, characterizing the topological structure of the universal operator class and constructing minimal invariant subspaces.
motivation: The invariant subspace problem remains a central open question in operator theory; the authors explore the structural consequences for universal operators if the answer is negative, and seek to understand the norm topology of the universal operator class independently.
method: Operator-theoretic arguments on separable complex Hilbert spaces: construction of minimal infinite-dimensional invariant subspaces under a negative ISP assumption, identification of Caradus–Pozzi and semi-Fredholm classes, plus affine composition operators on Hardy space H^2(D) via inner-outer factorization techniques.
result: Every universal operator has a continuum of pairwise trivially-intersecting minimal invariant subspaces whose restrictions are invertible with any prescribed geometric power decay; the norm interior, closure, and boundary of the universal operator class are identified as the Caradus–Pozzi class, the complement of the upper semi-Fredholm class, and operators that are neither upper nor lower semi-Fredholm, respectively.
conclusion: The results give a sharp topological and structural picture of universal operators, with explicit restrictions on generators of affine composition operators on H^2(D), independent of any resolution of the invariant subspace problem.

title: Synthesis Of The Transient Behaviour Of Optimization Algorithms For Strongly Convex Objective Functions
authors: Adel Abdelsamed, Dennis Gramlich, Christian Ebenbauer, Carsten W. Scherer
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the transient behavior of first-order optimization methods for unconstrained minimization of smooth and strongly convex objective functions. These methods are modelled as linear systems over finite-time intervals embedded in feedback with the gradient nonlinearity. By characterizing the function class through discrete-time Zames-Falb integral quadratic constraints, we employ a robust [MATH] control framework to obtain convex semidefinite programs certifying tight worst-case bounds on the terminal distance to the optimizer. Building on the same formulation, we derive a convex synthesis procedure for a transient-optimal method that achieves the optimal finite-horizon bounds and guarantees error reduction over any prescribed number of steps. The framework naturally extends to delayed gradient measurements, enabling both transient performance analysis and synthesis of optimal algorithms under feedback delays.
tldr: The paper uses robust control theory and discrete-time Zames-Falb integral quadratic constraints to analyze and synthesize transient-optimal first-order optimization algorithms for smooth strongly convex objectives.
motivation: First-order optimization methods lack tight worst-case guarantees on finite-horizon transient behavior, and existing analyses do not provide a systematic way to design algorithms that are optimal over a prescribed number of steps.
method: Methods are modeled as linear systems in feedback with the gradient nonlinearity over finite-time intervals, with the function class characterized by Zames-Falb IQCs, yielding convex semidefinite programs for both analysis and algorithm synthesis, extended to delayed gradients.
result: The framework certifies tight worst-case bounds on terminal distance to the optimizer and produces a transient-optimal method achieving optimal finite-horizon bounds with guaranteed error reduction, also covering feedback delays.
conclusion: Robust control with IQCs provides a unified convex framework for analyzing and designing transient-optimal optimization algorithms, with natural extensions to delay settings.

title: On The Complexification Of $ Q $-deformations Of Compact Semisimple Lie Groups
authors: Christian Voigt Heon Lee
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For the quantised algebra of functions on a simply connected compact semisimple Lie group, we study the relationship between the primitive spectrum, topologically irreducible representations by bounded operators on Hilbert spaces, and quantum holomorphic evaluations induced via the Drinfeld double. In terms of the Joseph stratification of the primitive spectrum, we prove a sharp dichotomy: primitive ideals in homogeneous strata always arise as kernels of topologically irreducible representations by bounded operators on a Hilbert space, whereas those in inhomogeneous strata do not admit any such realisations. We further show that, unlike in the classical situation, quantum holomorphic evaluations typically fail to be topologically irreducible, and that their kernels do not determine the primitive spectrum. Finally, we describe the Iwasawa decomposition of the Drinfeld double in terms of polynomial functions, extending work by Podle\'s-Woronowicz for the quantum Lorentz group to all complex semisimple quantum groups, and clarifying the structure of quantum holomorphic evaluations.
tldr: The paper studies complexifications of q-deformed function algebras on compact semisimple Lie groups, focusing on primitive spectra, irreducible Hilbert-space representations, and quantum holomorphic evaluations via the Drinfeld double.
motivation: The authors aim to clarify the representation theory and primitive ideal structure of quantized algebras of functions on compact semisimple Lie groups after complexification.
method: They analyze the Joseph stratification of the primitive spectrum and relate homogeneous versus inhomogeneous strata to kernels of topologically irreducible bounded Hilbert-space representations; they also describe an Iwasawa decomposition of the Drinfeld double.
result: They prove a sharp dichotomy: primitive ideals in homogeneous strata arise as kernels of topologically irreducible bounded representations, while those in inhomogeneous strata do not; quantum holomorphic evaluations typically fail to be topologically irreducible and do not determine the primitive spectrum.
conclusion: The work extends Podleś–Woronowicz results on the quantum Lorentz group to all complex semisimple quantum groups and clarifies the structure of quantum holomorphic evaluations.

title: Anytime Contracts For Ai Services
authors: Boris Velasevic, Eden Saig, Eric Mazumdar
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI services are prone to moral hazard, as model providers can silently route requests to cheaper, lower-quality models, and the inherent stochasticity of model outputs makes this degradation hard to detect. Contract theory addresses moral hazard by designing payment rules that reward high-quality outputs and prevent strategic overcharging. However, existing frameworks assume interactions of fixed duration, whereas AI services are typically consumed through subscriptions and pay-as-you-go APIs that users can terminate at any time based on observed performance. We show that this flexibility can break standard contracts, opening them up to abuse by either the providers or users. To address this, we extend contract theory to account for unknown exit rules. We formalize the problem as a Principal-Agent game, and show that budget-optimal contracts in this setting are proportional to anytime-valid hypothesis tests based on likelihood-ratio e-values. We give an efficient algorithm for computing anytime contracts and show how betting e-processes can be used to approximate them when the models are unknown. Finally, we evaluate our findings on synthetic data and data from deployed LLMs.
tldr: The paper extends contract theory to AI service markets with unknown, user-determined exit rules, showing that budget-optimal contracts correspond to anytime-valid hypothesis tests built from likelihood-ratio e-values.
motivation: AI service providers can silently route requests to cheaper, lower-quality models (moral hazard), and the stochasticity of model outputs makes such degradation hard to detect; existing contract frameworks assume fixed-duration interactions, whereas subscription and pay-as-you-go APIs let users terminate at any time.
method: The authors formalize the interaction as a Principal-Agent game with unknown stopping rules, derive budget-optimal anytime contracts proportional to anytime-valid tests based on likelihood-ratio e-values, give an efficient algorithm for computing them, and use betting e-processes to approximate them when models are unknown.
result: Flexibility in termination can break standard contracts and enable abuse by either providers or users; the proposed anytime contracts restore incentive guarantees, and are validated on synthetic data and data from deployed LLMs.
conclusion: Anytime-valid inference provides the right mathematical language for designing robust service contracts under strategic behavior and unpredictable user exit, bridging contract theory with modern e-value-based statistics.

title: Cryptographically Secure Agent-to-Agent Communication In Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Karol Budzyn, Adrian Brodzik, Mateusz Szczepkowski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23078v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) comprise AI agents that collaborate or compete to perform complex, distributed tasks. Their dynamic interactions create opportunities for threat actors to target and impersonate other agents, intercept messages, inject malicious prompts, and exfiltrate sensitive data while simultaneously complicating the detection of anomalous behavior through conventional monitoring. This paper surveys threats and cryptographic challenges in agent-to-agent communication and presents a zero-trust architecture integrating identity, transport security, message integrity, and monitoring. The architecture establishes agent identities via decentralized identifiers and task-scoped verifiable credentials backed by a permissioned ledger, enforcing least-privilege authorization. For transport security, it provides mutually authenticated, crypto-agile TLS with hybrid post-quantum key establishment, and evaluates KEMTLS with pre-distributed public keys to reduce handshake overhead. Signed CBOR envelopes preserve payload integrity across multi-hop exchanges, while zero-knowledge proofs verify declared task constraints without exposing underlying inputs. Context-aware monitoring of inter-agent messages, tool activity, and execution telemetry informs the setting of risk-based trust thresholds and supports the detection of behavioral anomalies. Together, these mechanisms provide an integrated framework for securing and auditing agent communication, with implications for other agentic protocols and prospective 6G semantic communication.
tldr: The paper surveys security threats in multi-agent AI communication and proposes a zero-trust architecture using decentralized identities, post-quantum TLS, signed CBOR envelopes, zero-knowledge proofs, and context-aware monitoring.
motivation: Multi-agent systems introduce new attack surfaces such as agent impersonation, message interception, prompt injection, and data exfiltration, while making anomalous behavior harder to detect with conventional monitoring.
method: The authors present a zero-trust architecture combining decentralized identifiers, verifiable credentials, permissioned-ledger-backed authorization, crypto-agile mutually authenticated TLS with hybrid post-quantum key establishment, KEMTLS evaluation, signed CBOR envelopes, zero-knowledge constraint verification, and risk-based monitoring.
result: The paper provides an integrated framework for securing and auditing agent-to-agent communication, with discussion of reducing handshake overhead and verifying task constraints without exposing underlying inputs.
conclusion: The proposed architecture aims to improve security and auditability in multi-agent systems, with potential implications for agentic protocols and 6G semantic communication.

title: Sieve-free ReLU Bayesian Priors With Near-minimax Posterior Contraction
authors: Hien Duy Nguyen, Jacob Westerhout, Julyan Arbel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish fractional-posterior contraction for shallow ReLU networks in Gaussian random-design regression with a [MATH]-H\"older target, using priors independent of the sample size and smoothness parameters. For any fixed design law [MATH] on [MATH], we obtain contraction in R\'enyi divergence and, after clipping posterior draws at a bound on the target range, in squared [MATH] loss at rate [MATH]. This matches the classical H\"older minimax rate up to a logarithmic factor. These priors have random finite width and use width-dependent uniform or Gaussian weight distributions, or width-independent Student [MATH] distributions, including Cauchy distributions.
tldr: The paper proves fractional-posterior contraction rates for shallow ReLU Bayesian neural networks in Gaussian random-design regression, matching Hölder minimax rates up to a logarithmic factor with sieve-free priors.
motivation: Bayesian neural networks typically require sample-size- and smoothness-dependent priors or sieves to obtain optimal posterior contraction; the authors aim to remove such dependencies while retaining near-minimax guarantees.
method: They construct priors with random finite width and width-dependent uniform/Gaussian weights (or width-independent Student-t weights such as Cauchy) and derive contraction in Rényi divergence, plus squared L2 loss after clipping posterior draws to the target range.
result: For any fixed design law and an alpha-Hölder target, the fractional posterior contracts at the classical Hölder minimax rate up to a logarithmic factor, without priors tuned to sample size or smoothness.
conclusion: Sieve-free, smoothness-agnostic priors can achieve near-optimal adaptive contraction for shallow ReLU networks, simplifying Bayesian nonparametric modeling of regression functions.

title: General Relativity In Three Lines
authors: Pawel Nurowski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22396v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that complex general relativity can be formulated directly in terms of three affine lines assigned to each spacetime point. The lines are represented by Pl\"ucker bivectors, and Urbantke's construction applied to the associated two-forms reconstructs the conformal spacetime metric. Starting from the chiral Pleba\'nski action, the simplicity constraints turn the three two-forms into a null internal basis of simple bivectors and thereby into three projective lines. A [MATH] decomposition then yields a first-order canonical theory whose configuration variable is the weighted triple of lines and whose conjugate variable is a line momentum. The resulting constraint system consists of three internal Gauss constraints, three vector constraints, and one Hamiltonian constraint. A notable feature of the line formulation is that the equation obtained by varying the line momentum is pointwise algebraic after the spatial integrations by parts. Consequently the momentum can be eliminated explicitly wherever the corresponding Legendre map is invertible, giving a second-order action whose only dynamical configuration variable is the weighted triple of lines. The line curvature separates naturally into a cosmological trace and the Weyl matrix of the selected chiral sector. The Legendre map becomes singular on a distinguished null-evolution locus where the spacetime metric remains nondegenerate. There its rank drops from nine to six, giving three algebraic compatibility conditions. We construct a finite invariant partial Legendre transform and a smooth constrained second-order continuation through this locus. This analysis provides a regular framework for regimes in which the evolution direction becomes null and may be useful in the study of near-horizon geometries and related gravitational phenomena.
tldr: The paper reformulates complex general relativity in terms of three projective/affine lines per spacetime point, deriving a first-order canonical theory and a second-order action with a regular continuation through a singular Legendre locus.
motivation: The authors aim to express complex GR directly in terms of chiral, line-valued variables (Plücker bivectors) so that the resulting constraint system and Legendre structure remain regular even where the evolution direction becomes null, as in near-horizon regimes.
method: Starting from the chiral Plebański action, simplicity constraints reduce the three two-forms to a null internal basis of simple bivectors, i.e. three projective lines; a 3+1 decomposition then yields a canonical theory with three Gauss, three vector, and one Hamiltonian constraint, with the line momentum eliminated when the Legendre map is invertible.
result: The momentum equation is pointwise algebraic after integration by parts, giving a second-order action in the weighted triple of lines alone; the line curvature splits into a cosmological trace and a Weyl matrix, and on the null-evolution locus the Legendre map drops rank from nine to six, producing three compatibility conditions that are resolved by a finite invariant partial Legendre transform.
conclusion: The line formulation provides a regular framework for spacetimes whose evolution direction becomes null and may be useful for studying near-horizon geometries and related gravitational phenomena.

title: Programming The Nonlinear Optics Of A Nanoporous Photonic Metamaterial By Confined Crystallization
authors: Andrii Z. Maxym, Junhui Lang, Bouchta Sahraoui, Anatoliy S. Andrushchak, Yaroslav Shchur, Olha Kityk, Robert Wielgosz, Monika Lelonek, Piotr Pawlik, Patrick Huber, Jaroslaw Jedryka, Andriy V. Kityk
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A membrane traversed by a dense array of nanochannels acts as a photonic metamaterial: with channels far smaller than the wavelength of light, the optical response is set by the architecture rather than by the constituent materials. Here each nanochannel is turned into a nonlinear optical meta-atom by filling anodic aluminum oxide (AAO) with benzil (BZL), a noncentrosymmetric molecular crystal, and the crystallization pathway programs their orientation. In free-standing membranes every channel solidifies independently, the orientations remain uncorrelated, and the effective second-harmonic generation (SHG) response is nearly polarization isotropic; its magnitude follows a core - shell model in which an optically inactive interfacial layer of 2.6 nm reduces the active volume of each meta-atom, reproducing on bare alumina the value previously found on alkyl-grafted silica and indicating a host-insensitive limit. Seeding crystallization from a bulk benzil layer instead aligns the meta-atoms over submillimeter domains and produces a macroscopically anisotropic effective susceptibility. Channel diameters from 32 to 270 nm span the transition out of the subwavelength regime, and the anomalous directional SHG emission reported here is confined to the metamaterial limit. Confined crystallization thus offers a route to nonlinear optical metamaterials whose effective susceptibility tensor is written during processing.
tldr: Filling anodic aluminum oxide nanochannels with the molecular crystal benzil turns each channel into a nonlinear-optical meta-atom whose orientation, and thus the effective second-harmonic susceptibility tensor, is programmed by the crystallization pathway.
motivation: The authors aim to show that a nanochannel membrane can act as a photonic metamaterial in which the optical response is dictated by channel architecture rather than constituent materials, and to demonstrate control over the nonlinear response by controlling confined crystallization.
method: Benzil is crystallized inside AAO nanochannels (32-270 nm diameters) in free-standing membranes and in seeded geometries; polarization-resolved SHG measurements characterize the effective susceptibility, interpreted with a core-shell model including an inactive 2.6 nm interfacial layer.
result: Unseeded growth gives uncorrelated orientations and nearly polarization-isotropic SHG described by the core-shell model, while seeding from a bulk benzil layer aligns meta-atoms over submillimeter domains and yields a macroscopically anisotropic effective susceptibility, with anomalous directional SHG confined to the subwavelength (metamaterial) regime.
conclusion: Confined crystallization offers a processing route to nonlinear optical metamaterials whose effective susceptibility tensor is written during fabrication.

title: Decomposing Urllc Deadline Failures In Beam-Managed 6g Networks: Implications For Mission-Critical Wireless Systems
authors: Sneihil Gopal Webert Montlouis
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22411v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mission-critical wireless systems require ultra-reliable low-latency communications (URLLC), which sixth-generation (6G) millimeter-wave (mmWave) beam-managed networks are designed to provide. However, the reported URLLC deadline miss rate often masks the specific causes of packet failures. This paper introduces a framework that categorizes missed URLLC packets into three causes: queueing-limited (Q), transmission-limited (T), and beam-tracking-limited (B). Our analysis across ten scenarios with antenna counts from [MATH] to [MATH] reveals three key findings. First, the dominant cause of missed packets shifts from Q to B when the antenna count exceeds roughly [MATH]. Therefore, operators of hyper-massive arrays should focus on improving beam-tracking accuracy to reduce the miss rate. Second, the beam-sweep period ([MATH]) significantly affects B-misses, while Q and T remain relatively unchanged. Reducing [MATH] from [MATH]ms to [MATH]ms can cut the B-misses by more than half, without requiring a redesign of the scheduler. Third, Q-misses reach a cumulative distribution function (CDF) of approximately [MATH] by [MATH]ms, so modest latency-budget relaxation can accommodate most overruns. In contrast, B-misses remain unsaturated at [MATH]ms, making them difficult to accommodate within practical application-layer latency limits. Overall, this framework transforms an ambiguous aggregate miss-rate metric into a clear three-way diagnostic tool that directly informs remedial actions for network operators.
tldr: A diagnostic framework that decomposes URLLC deadline miss rates in beam-managed 6G mmWave networks into queueing-limited, transmission-limited, and beam-tracking-limited failure causes.
motivation: Aggregate URLLC deadline miss-rate metrics obscure the underlying causes of packet failure, making it hard for operators of mission-critical wireless systems to choose effective remedies.
method: Simulation-based analysis across ten scenarios with varying antenna counts, categorizing missed packets into three causes and studying the impact of beam-sweep period on each category.
result: The dominant miss cause shifts from queueing to beam-tracking above a threshold antenna count; shortening the beam-sweep period halves beam-tracking misses; queueing misses saturate while beam-tracking misses remain unsaturated at practical latency limits.
conclusion: The three-way decomposition turns an ambiguous aggregate metric into an actionable diagnostic tool for 6G network operators, though the work is purely classical communications engineering.

title: Uav Rotatable Antenna Under Rotation Delay
authors: Yinmei Xie, Chiya Zhang, Chunlong He, Weizheng Zhang, Wei Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22777v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rotatable antennas (RAs) can improve wireless link performance by adjusting their boresight directions.
