conclusion: The work advances the generic positive-mass finiteness problem for planar six-body central configurations, while exceptional positive mass loci remain for Part II.

title: Recoverability-Controlled Safety Miscalibration In Large Language Models
authors: Yuwei Wang, Xingwang Liang, Yu Xie, Haotian Chi, Haijun Geng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety-aligned language models are expected to refuse harmful requests while remaining useful for benign ones. However, because many evaluations score only the final response, they often conflate intent understanding with response-level safety behavior. To address this, we introduce RiskCueBench, a recoverability-controlled benchmark that separates these two stages by first measuring whether a model can successfully recover a high-level intent and then evaluating its safety behavior on the same prompt. RiskCueBench contains 160 latent intents and 640 abstract non-operational surface prompts across eight risk categories. The benchmark covers 25 completed model groups and 32,000 successful model outputs with final rubric-adjudicated labels. When conditioning on pairs where both surface forms are recoverable, we find that increased contextualized specificity induces a shift toward less safe behavior. Specifically, paired bootstrap estimates show that the refusal rate and global safety score decrease by 0.175 and 0.440, respectively. Furthermore, mixed effects modeling corroborates a 0.107 increase in unsafe cooperation. These results show that the safety behavior can be miscalibrated to the surface form even after the intent has been recovered, motivating safety evaluations that report response behavior conditional on semantic recoverability.
tldr: RiskCueBench is a recoverability-controlled benchmark that separates a language model's ability to recover a latent harmful intent from its downstream safety behavior on the same prompt.
motivation: Existing safety evaluations score only final responses, conflating intent understanding with response-level refusal behavior and thus obscuring where safety failures actually arise.
method: The authors build a benchmark of 160 latent intents rendered into 640 abstract, non-operational surface prompts across eight risk categories, then evaluate 25 model groups (32,000 outputs) with rubric-adjudicated labels, conditioning analyses on pairs where both surface forms are recoverable and applying paired bootstrap and mixed-effects modeling.
result: Conditioning on recoverable pairs, increased contextualized specificity lowers the refusal rate by 0.175 and the global safety score by 0.440, while unsafe cooperation rises by 0.107.
conclusion: Safety behavior can be miscalibrated to surface form even after intent is recovered, motivating evaluations that report response behavior conditional on semantic recoverability.

title: An Agentic Enf Framework For Forensic Video Authentication Against Generative Ai
authors: Bacha Rehman Ryan Wyton (southampton Solent University)
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative models now synthesise video that is hard to distinguish from genuine footage, and learned detectors that key on a generator's artefacts degrade sharply on unseen models. This paper develops a forensic framework that authenticates video by a signal that generation does not control: the electric network frequency (ENF), the mains-driven hum in audio and flicker in video. A unified two-channel detector extracts the ENF from audio and from rolling-shutter video through one second harmonic estimator and a shared network; a synthetic-injection training method, driven by an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck drift model and anchored to real recordings, overcomes the scarcity of labelled ENF data; a reference-matching channel verifies a claimed time of recording and recovers an unknown one; and a two-axis agentic orchestrator fuses recording authenticity with content-manipulation evidence under an asymmetric rule, escalating expensive detectors only when needed. A central finding reframes the task: an ENF-band flicker is present in generated video at a prominence indistinguishable from real footage, so its presence is not proof of authenticity, and authentication must rest on consistency with an independent reference rather than on presence. On held-out real recordings the detector accepts genuine audio and video at 93% and 100% against naive baselines of 53% and 15%; claimed-time authentication reaches an area under the curve of 1.0; and the agentic cascade matches a flat ensemble while cutting wall-clock time by 54% and frames decoded by 64%, without loss of accuracy.
tldr: The paper presents an agentic forensic framework that authenticates video by extracting electric network frequency (ENF) signals from audio and rolling-shutter flicker, combining them in a cascaded detector to defend against generative-AI video forgery.
motivation: Generative models can now synthesize highly realistic video, and learned artifact-based detectors generalize poorly to unseen generators, so a forensic signal that generation does not control—the mains-driven ENF hum and flicker—is exploited instead.
method: A unified two-channel detector extracts ENF from audio and video via a shared second-harmonic estimator and network, trained with synthetic ENF injection based on an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck drift model anchored to real recordings; a reference-matching channel verifies or recovers recording time, and a two-axis agentic orchestrator fuses authenticity and manipulation evidence under an asymmetric escalation rule.
result: On held-out real recordings the detector accepts genuine audio and video at 93% and 100% (versus naive baselines of 53% and 15%), claimed-time authentication achieves AUC 1.0, and the agentic cascade matches a flat ensemble while cutting wall-clock time by 54% and decoded frames by 64%; notably, ENF-band flicker appears in generated video at real-like prominence, so presence alone is not proof of authenticity.
conclusion: ENF-based authentication should rest on consistency with an independent reference rather than mere presence of the signal, and the proposed agentic cascade offers an efficient, accurate forensic tool for video provenance.

title: What It Is, Not What It Says: Securing Agentic Browsing Interactions With Web Semantics
authors: Umar Iqbal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents increasingly browse the web on users' behalf, yet they consume webpages as screenshots or text, exposing their LLMs to unvetted third-party content. Browsers enforce semantics under which what an element can do depends on what it is and where it comes from, not on what it says. Agents flatten these semantics, so injected text can persuade the LLM to exercise the user's authority for content that has none. As LLMs remain easy to persuade, the agent's interface to the web must itself ensure the integrity of what the agent reads, interprets, and does. We propose Intact, which runs on an unmodified browser. Intact builds GenTree, a bespoke representation that captures provenance and web semantics. Intact passes the page via GenTree to the LLM one element at a time, so the LLM decides on each element without any other element's text. Its harness executes each step only within the capabilities of the step's element and asks the user before acting on third-party content. On 1,270 real webpages, GenTree attributes 2.3x as many elements to third parties as the browser, which misattributes 58.7% of them to the first party. On 1,091 of these webpages with injected attacks, only 12.8% of attacks get through Intact's planner, each at most as a consent request, against 73.1% for a conventional planner. Isolation disrupts functionality on only 3.7% of tasks, and a parallel schedule could remove most of its added latency.
tldr: Intact is a browser-based system that preserves web semantics and provenance through a bespoke 'GenTree' representation so that LLM browsing agents act on what elements are rather than on injected text, reducing prompt-injection attacks.
motivation: AI agents browsing the web consume pages as screenshots or flat text, flattening browser security semantics and exposing their LLMs to unvetted third-party content that can hijack the user's authority.
method: Intact runs on an unmodified browser, builds a provenance-aware semantic tree (GenTree) of the page, presents elements to the LLM one at a time in isolation, executes each step only within the capabilities of that element, and asks the user before acting on third-party content.
result: Across 1,270 real webpages GenTree attributes 2.3x more elements to third parties than the browser (which misattributes 58.7% to the first party); on 1,091 pages with injected attacks only 12.8% of attacks penetrate the planner (at most as consent requests) versus 73.1% for a conventional planner, with functionality disruption on only 3.7% of tasks.
conclusion: Enforcing web semantics and provenance integrity at the agent's interface substantially improves the security of agentic browsing at modest functional cost, with parallel scheduling able to mitigate added latency.

title: Cooperation Without Adaptation: Llm Agents In A Collective-Risk Dilemma
authors: Trung-Kiet Huynh, Dao-Sy Duy-Minh, Chi-Nguyen Tran, Phu-Hoa Pham, Phu-Quy Nguyen-Lam, Le Hong Trang, The Anh Han
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed to act on behalf of people in settings where individual decisions shape shared outcomes. We examine whether five production models adapt their contributions to changing risks and partner behaviour, or instead follow a relatively fixed strategy. In a collective-risk dilemma game (CRG), six players contribute to a shared pool over ten rounds; if the pool falls short of its target, a catastrophe may destroy their remaining resources. Four models contributed approximately an equal share at every positive risk level, and four of the five also contributed when risk was zero, even though contributing could not improve their payoff. Explicitly stating that only the agent's own payoff mattered reduced zero-risk contributions for most models, while a more neutral prompt did not. Several models correctly identified which action offered the higher expected payoff at different risk levels, yet their contributions changed little. Against fixed partners, no model consistently chose the payoff-maximising response, and in mixed-model groups, a single agent's shortfall in the final round could cause an otherwise successful group to fail. Payoff-based selection also depended on population composition: in a single six-agent group, it favoured the model that contributed least and reduced group success, whereas in larger, randomly mixed populations, it favoured an exact fair-share model at moderate and high risk. These findings show that cooperative self-play alone is not evidence of strategic adaptability. Consistent with a machine-behaviour approach, evaluations of agents in multi-agent systems should test how they respond to incentives, partner actions, and population composition.
tldr: Five production LLM agents are tested in a ten-round collective-risk dilemma game to see whether they adapt contributions to risk levels, partner behaviour, and payoff incentives, or instead follow fixed cooperative heuristics.
motivation: LLM agents increasingly act on behalf of humans in settings with shared outcomes, so it matters whether their cooperative behaviour is genuinely strategic and incentive-responsive rather than a fixed disposition acquired from self-play training.
method: Six-player CRG experiments with five commercial models across varying catastrophe risk levels, prompt framings (neutral vs. self-payoff emphasis), fixed partner strategies, and mixed-model populations of differing composition and size.
result: Most models contributed a near-constant equal share regardless of risk, often contributing even at zero risk where it was payoff-dominated; explicit self-interest prompts reduced this, and models frequently identified the payoff-maximising action without acting on it, while payoff-based selection in small groups favoured low contributors and reduced group success.
conclusion: Cooperative self-play performance is not evidence of strategic adaptability, and agent evaluations in multi-agent systems should probe responses to incentives, partner actions, and population composition.

title: SAFE-Mem: Secure Agentic Memory With Fine-Grained Authority And Governance-Aware Retrieval
authors: Haoming Li, Dingyi Kang, Xu Hu, Jinxin Yang, Zhu Xu, Chenru Wang, Yi Ge, Miao Yin, Guanpeng Li, Feng Chen, Bingzhe Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on persistent memory to support long-term reasoning and personalized interactions. However, information collected from external sources can introduce security risks when untrusted claims (i.e., atomic statements) are later treated as authorized preferences, policies, or permissions. Existing defenses typically rely on content-based filtering or coarse-grained provenance tracking, which either fail to prevent unauthorized memory use or block legitimate information, sacrificing memory utility. To address these limitations, we propose SAFE-Mem, a fine-grained memory governance framework that improves security while preserving legitimate memory use. First, SAFE-Mem annotates each claim with three governance labels (i.e., kind, authority, and scope) to capture its provenance and permitted use. Second, governance-aware retrieval matches query requirements with claim permissions to block unauthorized influence while retaining legitimate information. Third, a governance-enabled memory graph connects source sentences, claims, and entities to support provenance tracking and efficient retrieval. Across four LLM backbones on MPBench and LoCoMo, SAFE-Mem attains the lowest attack success among defenses that retain legitimate memory, at least 77% below the strongest of them, and the highest answer accuracy of all evaluated defenses, improving it by up to 15%. The code is available at [URL].
tldr: SAFE-Mem is a governance framework that secures LLM agent memory by labeling claims with provenance and authority metadata and enforcing these labels during retrieval.
motivation: Persistent memory in LLM agents lets untrusted external claims be mistaken for authorized preferences or permissions, while existing content filtering and coarse provenance tracking either fail to block misuse or over-block legitimate information.
method: Each atomic claim is annotated with three governance labels (kind, authority, scope); governance-aware retrieval matches query requirements against claim permissions, and a governance-enabled memory graph links source sentences, claims, and entities for provenance tracking.
result: Across four LLM backbones on MPBench and LoCoMo, SAFE-Mem achieves the lowest attack success rate among utility-preserving defenses (at least 77% below the strongest baseline) and the highest answer accuracy, improving it by up to 15%.
conclusion: Fine-grained, governance-aware memory management can substantially improve the security of agentic memory without sacrificing legitimate memory utility.

title: Proportionality In Ranking Compression
authors: Daniel Halpern, Xinyu Liu, Evi Micha, Yu Peng Ng, Warut Suksompong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23193v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by applications in reinforcement learning from human feedback, we consider a setting where a given collection of rankings needs to be compressed into a smaller collection of rankings. This can also be seen as a combination of two fundamental social choice frameworks: ranking aggregation and multiwinner voting. We propose three proportionality notions that capture different types of representation in this setting: positional proportionality, pairwise proportionality, and proportionality for solid coalitions (PSC). On the one hand, we show that positional proportionality and PSC are always satisfiable for any input rankings and target compression size, and a desired output can be found in polynomial time. On the other hand, we prove that pairwise proportionality cannot be satisfied in general, but can nevertheless be attained when the input rankings are single-peaked or single-crossing.
tldr: The paper studies how to compress a collection of rankings into a smaller set while preserving proportionality, formalizing three notions (positional, pairwise, and PSC) and analyzing their satisfiability and computational complexity.
motivation: Motivated by reinforcement learning from human feedback, where large sets of rankings must be summarized, the authors bridge ranking aggregation and multiwinner voting to define fair representation in compressed rankings.
method: They introduce three proportionality axioms for ranking compression—positional proportionality, pairwise proportionality, and proportionality for solid coalitions (PSC)—and analyze existence and polynomial-time construction for each.
result: Positional proportionality and PSC are always satisfiable with polynomial-time algorithms, whereas pairwise proportionality is not generally satisfiable but becomes attainable for single-peaked or single-crossing inputs.
conclusion: The work provides a social-choice-theoretic foundation for fair ranking compression, characterizing which proportionality guarantees can be achieved and under what preference restrictions.

title: Geometric Multigrid Preconditioners For Unfitted Discretisations Of The De Rham Complex
authors: Jordi Manyer Santiago Badia
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose two families of multigrid preconditioners for unfitted finite element discretisations of the Riesz maps of the de Rham complex, in H(grad), H(curl) and H(div), stabilised by cell aggregation. The first is a geometric multigrid method applied directly to the unfitted operators, on a hierarchy of background meshes that share the same boundary representation. Its smoothers are star patches built on the aggregated mesh, so that each patch captures the kernel of the stabilisation. The second is a multilevel auxiliary-space preconditioner that combines a patch smoother localised around the cut cells with the body-fitted problem on the active mesh, which is in turn solved by a non-nested geometric multigrid method. Both are used as building blocks of block-diagonal preconditioners for the mixed Hodge Laplacians. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions, on geometries with a controlled cut fraction and on general geometries, show iteration counts that are robust with respect to the cut configuration, the mesh size and the number of levels. We also report results for higher-order discretisations, weakly imposed Dirichlet boundary conditions and a face-based stabilisation.
tldr: The paper develops geometric multigrid and auxiliary-space preconditioners for unfitted finite element discretisations of de Rham complex Riesz maps and mixed Hodge Laplacians.
motivation: Unfitted finite element methods for the de Rham complex require robust solvers that handle cut cells and stabilisation without sacrificing scalability.
method: Two preconditioner families are proposed: a geometric multigrid method on background mesh hierarchies with star-patch smoothers, and a multilevel auxiliary-space preconditioner combining cut-cell patch smoothing with body-fitted solves on the active mesh.
result: Numerical experiments in 2D and 3D show iteration counts robust with respect to cut configuration, mesh size, and number of levels, including higher-order discretisations and weakly imposed Dirichlet conditions.
conclusion: The proposed multigrid preconditioners provide robust and scalable solvers for unfitted de Rham complex discretisations and mixed Hodge Laplacian problems.

title: Time-optimal Vaccination In State-dependent Sir Models: A Single Switch Criterion And Numerical Examples Outside Its Regime
authors: Yeachan Park, Jiwoong Jang, Yeoneung Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23095v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a susceptible, infected, and recovered (SIR) model with constant rates, a time-optimal vaccination policy has at most one switch from no vaccination to maximal vaccination. We allow the transmission and recovery rates [MATH] and [MATH] to depend on the state. If [MATH] and [MATH] throughout the forward invariant state space, then every optimal control is bang-bang with at most one switch. The incidence condition allows the transmission coefficient to decrease with prevalence. The Pontryagin analysis shows that [MATH], the sensitivity of per capita infected growth to the susceptible fraction, and the infected costate together determine the crossing direction of the switching function. We also prove existence of an optimal control, derive explicit a priori upper bounds on the eradication time and characterize the switching time by an optimization over one variable. For parameter sets that violate [MATH], numerical optimization gives controls with two switches and smaller eradication times than the computed minima over the single switch family. These computations provide a reproducible numerical counterexample to an unrestricted single switch claim. In a prescribed parameter sweep satisfying [MATH], delayed vaccination reduces the eradication time relative to immediate full vaccination by more than [MATH] in [MATH] of the cases, with a maximum reduction of [MATH]. In examples near this maximum, the delay increases peak prevalence by more than an order of magnitude and cumulative incidence more than fourfold. Hence minimizing eradication time does not in general minimize epidemiological burden.
tldr: This paper studies time-optimal vaccination policies in state-dependent SIR epidemic models and derives a single-switch bang-bang criterion, along with numerical counterexamples where two switches outperform single-switch controls.
motivation: In constant-rate SIR models, optimal vaccination policies have at most one switch, and the authors ask whether this structural claim survives when transmission and recovery rates depend on the epidemiological state.
method: Pontryagin's maximum principle is applied to state-dependent SIR dynamics to characterize the switching function through the sensitivity of per-capita infected growth to the susceptible fraction and the infected costate; existence of an optimal control and a priori eradication-time bounds are proven, supplemented by numerical optimization over parameter sweeps.
result: Under the incidence condition every optimal control is bang-bang with at most one switch, and the switching time reduces to a one-variable optimization; outside this regime, numerical optimization finds two-switch controls with strictly smaller eradication times, and delayed vaccination can shorten eradication time substantially while increasing peak prevalence by over an order of magnitude.
conclusion: Minimizing eradication time does not generally minimize epidemiological burden, and the unrestricted single-switch claim fails for state-dependent rates.

title: Erase The Mark, Preserve The Motion: Temporally Consistent Removal Of Video Watermarks
authors: Yifan Liao, Zhen Sun, Zhicong Huang, Jiaming He, Zongmin Zhang, Xi Ai, Cheng Hong, Xinhu Zheng, Xinlei He
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in video generation have increased the demand for reliable watermarking for copyright protection, yet the robustness of video watermarks against removal attacks remains underexplored. Most watermark-removal methods originate from the image domain: signal optimization injects imperceptible pixel-domain perturbations, whereas generative resynthesis produces a visually similar instance through diffusion synthesis. When extended to videos, the former introduces temporally varying noise that causes visible flickering, while the latter regenerates fine-grained structures inconsistently across frames, leading to structural motion inconsistency. To evaluate video watermark robustness, we propose PoseRegen, a pose-consistent reconstruction framework that removes watermarks while preserving the original content and motion. PoseRegen first applies a temporally shared viewpoint transformation to disrupt watermark-bearing spatial patterns and then jointly reconstructs the transformed sequence with a pose-conditioned video model. A frozen video DiT processes the complete sequence with its reference-video latent, and full-sequence Flow Matching supervision keeps identity and background consistent across frames. To further preserve motion structure, we introduce a lightweight Pose-Conditioned Motion Consistency Adapter that adapts the frozen backbone to temporally ordered pose guidance and constrains body-part trajectories throughout reconstruction. Experiments on eleven video watermarking schemes show that PoseRegen reduces the average bit accuracy to 0.505, near random guessing, while outperforming the strongest baseline by 9.34% on motion-related VBench metrics. These results reveal a practical vulnerability of current video watermarks and highlight the need to evaluate robustness jointly with temporal and motion quality.
tldr: PoseRegen is a pose-consistent reconstruction framework that removes video watermarks while preserving content and motion, exposing vulnerabilities in current video watermarking schemes.
motivation: Video watermark removal methods borrowed from images either introduce temporal flicker (pixel perturbation) or break motion consistency (per-frame diffusion resynthesis), and watermark robustness against such attacks is underexplored.
method: A temporally shared viewpoint transformation disrupts watermark patterns, followed by joint full-sequence reconstruction with a frozen pose-conditioned video DiT under Flow Matching supervision, plus a lightweight Pose-Conditioned Motion Consistency Adapter constraining body-part trajectories.
result: Across eleven video watermarking schemes, average bit accuracy drops to 0.505 (near random guessing), while motion-related VBench metrics improve by 9.34% over the strongest baseline.
conclusion: Current video watermarks are practically vulnerable, and robustness evaluation should be conducted jointly with temporal and motion quality.

title: Model-as-a-Trojan: Self-Activating Covert Dns Exfiltration Baked Into The Weights Of An Llm Agent
authors: Shaked Zychlinski Barak Haryati
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-weight models are downloaded from public hubs and run inside agent harnesses that grant them tools, most powerfully, a shell, under the assumption that a sandbox contains whatever the model might do. This paper demonstrates that the assumption has a blind spot: the weights themselves can be the malware, and the sandbox's last open door, DNS, is enough. We fine-tune an open-weight LLM so that a single covert behavior lives in its parameters: on the first turn of every conversation, whenever the model infers from its context that a shell tool is available, it emits one self-contained command that reads a secret from the runtime environment, base32-encodes it, chunks it, and exfiltrates it as DNS queries toward an attacker-controlled authoritative name server. It then answers the user normally and never mentions, or repeats, the act. Because the channel is DNS, the attack completes from inside a container with no internet egress beyond name resolution - measured payload-level and model-level behind an egress firewall that drops every non-DNS packet, with the secret reconstructed from the gateway resolver's query log. Because the behavior lives in the weights, prompting is the only off-switch a victim has, and it is unreliable: the implant fires in 20/20 of adversarial suppression trials, deflects direct interrogation without disclosing the sequence, and sweeps a 45-cell sandbox-fault matrix across five tool-calling formats - plus a fresh post-training canary, persona-only and absent system prompts, and an egress-locked topology - with zero leaks and zero repeat fires. Every training trajectory is execution-verified in a real container, and every claimed exfiltration is proven resolver-side: we reconstruct the secret from the authoritative resolver's query log alone.
tldr: The authors fine-tune an open-weight LLM so that a covert DNS-exfiltration behavior is embedded directly in its weights, firing automatically when a shell tool is detected.
motivation: Sandboxed agent harnesses assume containment of model behavior, but the model weights themselves can act as malware; the paper tests whether DNS, the last permitted egress channel, suffices for data exfiltration.
method: A single covert behavior is trained into the model via execution-verified fine-tuning trajectories; the implant reads an environment secret, base32-encodes and chunks it, and exfiltrates it via DNS queries to an attacker-controlled authoritative nameserver, validated behind an egress firewall and reconstructed from resolver logs.
result: The implant fires in 20/20 adversarial suppression trials, resists direct interrogation, and shows zero leaks or repeat fires across a 45-cell sandbox-fault matrix and multiple tool-calling formats and prompt conditions.
conclusion: Model weights can serve as a self-activating malware channel that survives sandboxing, and prompting is an unreliable mitigation, highlighting a security blind spot in open-weight agent deployment.

title: A Physics-based And Geometry-aware Reduced-order Framework For Accelerated Part-Scale Thermomechanical Simulation Of Additive Friction Stir Deposition Process
authors: Sourav Saha Apurba Sarker
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Additive friction stir deposition (AFSD) is attractive for naval and aerospace sustainment because it enables high rate, solid state near net shape fabrication and repair of large metallic components. However, full part scale thermomechanical simulations remain computationally demanding because of the moving heat source, progressive material deposition, and evolving geometry. This work presents a physics-based and geometry-aware reduced order framework for rapid prediction of temperature and residual stress fields in part scale AFSD builds. The transient temperature field is represented using a tensor product quadratic B spline basis on a fixed Cartesian background grid, while arbitrary part geometries are embedded using a signed distance function (SDF) and a smooth material indicator. Residual stresses are recovered through an inherent strain formulation in which an offline thermo elasto plastic representative volume element (RVE) simulation supplies a calibrated eigenstrain field that is spatially scaled using the part scale peak temperature history. The thermal formulation is evaluated against published numerical and experimental AFSD data and two sample multilayer builds are simulated as demonstrations. For a four layer thin-wall build, the thermal solution requires approximately 22 s compared to 806 s for the finite element model, while the complete thermo-mechanical framework requires approximately 86.4 s compared to 2,406 s. For a larger 20 layer hollow cylindrical build, the reduced order thermal simulations requires 0.148 to 0.152 h compared with 1.8 h for the finite element model, corresponding to thermal speed-ups of approximately 11.8 to 12.2 times. The complete thermomechanical framework requires 0.346 h compared to 5.4 h for the full finite element analysis, providing an overall speed-up of approximately 15.6 times.
tldr: A physics-based, geometry-aware reduced-order modeling framework accelerates part-scale thermomechanical simulation of additive friction stir deposition by roughly 12-16x over finite element analysis.
motivation: Part-scale thermomechanical simulations of additive friction stir deposition are prohibitively expensive due to moving heat sources, progressive material deposition, and evolving geometry, motivating faster surrogate approaches for large metallic component fabrication and repair.
method: The transient temperature field is represented with tensor-product quadratic B-spline basis functions on a fixed Cartesian grid, with complex geometries embedded via a signed distance function and smooth material indicator; residual stresses are recovered from an inherent strain formulation calibrated by offline thermo-elasto-plastic RVE simulations and scaled by peak temperature history.
result: For a four-layer thin-wall build, thermal solve time dropped from 806 s (FEM) to about 22 s, and the full thermomechanical framework from 2,406 s to 86.4 s; a 20-layer hollow cylinder showed ~11.8-12.2x thermal speed-up and ~15.6x overall speed-up.
conclusion: The reduced-order framework enables rapid, reasonably accurate prediction of temperature and residual stress fields in part-scale AFSD builds, offering substantial computational savings suitable for large-component manufacturing and repair workflows.

title: Managing Complexity For Integrated Fusion Reactor Design Using A Differentiable Graph-based Mdao Framework: Process As A Case Study
authors: Timo J. Bogaarts, Willem Rutten, Felix Warmer
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22687v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated design of nuclear fusion reactors requires combining an increasingly large number of models from different disciplines self-consistently, with model selection and parametrisation changing between design studies. Manual definition of execution order and solvers for cyclic dependencies is error-prone, inefficient, and inflexible. We propose to use a generic graph-based coordination and execution core that enables automated execution order, cycle detection, and solver architecture specification for any set of models or parametrisation. To this end, a computational dependency graph of purely functional models is extended by a conditional node and nesting edges, treating solvers and optimisers in the same way. A minimal set of graph operations then allows for fine-tuned control on feedback resolution, making both optimiser and solver architectures easily reconfigurable. Existing monolithic multidisciplinary design analysis and optimisation (MDAO) architectures can be recovered by sequentially applying these operations. The cottax package implements this extended dependency graph, graph operations, executability checks, and a JAX-based execution layer. This execution layer eliminates runtime overhead and provides native gradient computation through the whole graph. As a proof of principle, cottax is then applied to the PROCESS systems code. Graph sequencing shows that for PROCESS only three small coupled components need to be solved every optimiser iteration. Monolithic MDAO architectures are then assigned to seven different PROCESS configurations, demonstrating the ease of (re)configuring its architecture. Compared to PROCESS, the sequencing and execution back-end together yield a two to three orders of magnitude reduction in model runtime during optimisation. cottax is currently being considered as the basis for developing an integrated stellarator MDAO framework.
tldr: The authors present cottax, a graph-based, differentiable MDAO coordination framework that automates execution ordering, cycle detection, and solver/optimiser composition for integrated fusion reactor design, demonstrated on the PROCESS systems code.
motivation: Integrated design of fusion reactors requires self-consistent coupling of many discipline-specific models whose selection and parametrisation vary between studies, making manual specification of execution order and cyclic-dependency solvers error-prone, slow, and inflexible.
method: They extend a computational dependency graph of purely functional models with a conditional node and nesting edges, define a small set of graph operations to reconfigure solver and optimiser architectures, and implement this in the cottax package with a JAX-based execution layer for native end-to-end gradients.
result: Applied to PROCESS, graph sequencing shows only three small coupled components need solving per optimiser iteration, monolithic MDAO architectures are recovered for seven PROCESS configurations, and runtime during optimisation drops by two to three orders of magnitude.
conclusion: The graph-based differentiable framework substantially simplifies and accelerates the (re)configuration of integrated design workflows and is being considered as the basis for an integrated stellarator MDAO framework.

title: Pinn-lpcdd: Physics-Informed Neural Network With Learnable And Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition For Compressible Multi-Medium Flows
authors: Weiheng Zeng, Hao Wang, Jiaxin Zhu, Kun Wang, Tiegang Liu, Chengliang Feng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The physics-informed neural network (PINN) faces significant challenges when solving compressible multi-medium flows, including the inability to locate interface positions, poor approximation of discontinuities, and difficulty in handling high-pressure-ratio problems between media with large stiffness differences. To address these issues, we propose PINN with Learnable and Physically Consistent Domain Decomposition (PINN-LPCDD), a framework that incorporates the sharp interface method (SIM) into PINNs for solving compressible multi-medium flows. Firstly, we design separate sub-networks for each medium with learnable parameters to automatically learn interface positions, so that the domain decomposition is physically consistent, and the contact discontinuity at the interface is naturally sharp. Secondly, the Euler equations with artificial viscosity are solved to enhance robustness when handling problems involving shock waves. Lastly, the scaling invariance of the Euler equations is exploited to facilitate the solution of high pressure ratio problems. Numerical experiments on air-air, air-helium, air-water, and air-R22 problems demonstrate the acceptable accuracy of the proposed method in simulating multi-medium flows.
tldr: PINN-LPCDD integrates a sharp interface method into physics-informed neural networks with learnable sub-networks to solve compressible multi-medium flows.
motivation: Standard PINNs struggle with compressible multi-medium flows: they cannot locate interfaces, poorly approximate discontinuities, and fail on high-pressure-ratio problems involving media with large stiffness differences.
method: The framework assigns a separate learnable sub-network to each medium to discover interface positions and enforce a physically consistent, sharp domain decomposition, solves Euler equations with artificial viscosity for shock robustness, and exploits scaling invariance of the Euler equations for high pressure ratios.
result: Numerical experiments on air-air, air-helium, air-water, and air-R22 problems show acceptable accuracy in simulating multi-medium flows.
conclusion: The proposed approach improves interface tracking and discontinuity handling in PINNs for multi-medium flow simulation, though it remains a classical computational physics contribution.

title: Stochastic Shockwave Dynamics In First-Order Traffic Flow
authors: Alireza Talebpour Yanlin Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23022v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Moving congestion fronts vary across realizations even when the traffic-flow law is fixed. This paper develops a generator-based formulation of the Lighthill--Whitham--Richards (LWR) model with random initial density and a deterministic fundamental diagram. Randomness enters through the initial spatial density field; every realization follows the same conservation law. For a smooth strictly concave fundamental diagram, we adapt established one-sided spatial Markov closure to traffic variables under the stated spatial-process and regularity assumptions, and derive a kinetic balance for physically normalized front intensities. Evolving the spatial generator provides density laws and congestion-front statistics without solving a road-grid problem for every realization. The formulation is continuous in physical space and time, while its numerical implementation approximates density state and integrates physical time. Four experiments distinguish deterministic consistency from stochastic comparison. Riemann and signal examples recover independently constructed exact LWR solutions. Smooth strictly concave approximations approach the deterministic triangular-diagram signal solution over the tested finite horizons; this does not establish stochastic closure at contacts or the capacity kink. A matched Monte Carlo Godunov ensemble evaluates front counts, sizes, mergers, and density distributions. The evolved generator also yields an instantaneous travel-time distribution for a frozen density field, compared with the same functional of the matched Godunov profiles. This quantity is not experienced travel time through evolving traffic. Resolution checks identify remaining normalization and small-front-loss effects. The contribution is direct evolution and interpretation of traffic-state and front distributions under a fixed first-order traffic law.
tldr: The paper develops a generator-based stochastic formulation of the Lighthill-Whitham-Richards first-order traffic flow model to compute congestion-front statistics under random initial density.
motivation: Congestion fronts in traffic flow vary across realizations even when the fundamental diagram is fixed, motivating a probabilistic description that avoids solving a road-grid problem for every realization.
method: Randomness is injected through the initial spatial density field while all realizations obey the same conservation law; a one-sided spatial Markov closure is adapted to traffic variables, and the spatial generator is evolved numerically and benchmarked against a matched Monte Carlo Godunov ensemble.
result: The scheme recovers exact LWR solutions for Riemann and signal examples, approaches the deterministic triangular-diagram solution under smooth strictly concave approximations, and yields front counts, sizes, mergers, density distributions, and instantaneous travel-time distributions.
conclusion: The contribution is direct evolution and interpretation of traffic-state and front distributions under a fixed first-order traffic law, with remaining normalization and small-front-loss effects noted.

title: On Exponential Stability Of Generalized Linear Functional Differential Equations
authors: Elena Braverman Leonid Berezansky
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22696v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a general approach to uniform exponential stability for a broad class of linear functional differential equations with Volterra operators. The considered class includes delay differential equations, integro-differential equations, equations with distributed delays, vector equations, and systems of scalar functional differential equations. Standard assumptions on the equation are relaxed to include measurable parameters. Some results remain valid for equations with unbounded delays and oscillatory coefficients and kernels. For all the above mentioned classes of equations, explicit uniform exponential stability tests are obtained.
tldr: The paper develops a general framework for uniform exponential stability tests for linear functional differential equations with Volterra operators, covering delay, integro-differential, and distributed-delay equations.
motivation: Existing stability criteria for functional differential equations rely on restrictive assumptions on parameters; the authors aim to relax these to measurable parameters and handle unbounded delays and oscillatory coefficients.
method: A unified operator-theoretic approach using Volterra operators yields explicit uniform exponential stability tests applicable across several classes of linear functional differential equations.
result: Explicit, verifiable exponential stability criteria are derived for delay differential equations, integro-differential equations, distributed-delay equations, and vector/scalar systems, including cases with unbounded delays and oscillatory kernels.
conclusion: The framework generalizes and unifies prior stability results while weakening standard assumptions, though the work is purely mathematical with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Solving The Tikhonov Regularization Of The Total Least Squares Problem By Matrix Simultaneous Diagonalization Via Congruence
authors: Thi Ngan Nguyen Van-Bong Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22880v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We are concerned with solving the Tikhonov regularization of the total least squares (TRTLS) which minimizes a sum of a quadratic fractional function and a nonnegative penalty quadratic form. If the penalty is nonsingular, the problem is attained and has been solved efficiently. However, if the penalty is singular, the problem becomes much more complicated, it may not be attained. In this paper we explore the property of simultaneously diagonalizable via congruence of matrices to make a change of variables and transform the problem into one of three tractable formats. Each of which is then thorough analyzed.
tldr: The paper solves the Tikhonov-regularized total least squares problem with a possibly singular penalty term by exploiting simultaneous diagonalization of matrices via congruence to reduce it to one of three tractable forms.
motivation: When the penalty in TRTLS is nonsingular the problem is well-posed and efficiently solvable, but a singular penalty makes the problem much harder and possibly unattained, motivating a structural reformulation.
method: Matrix simultaneous diagonalization via congruence is used to perform a change of variables that transforms the TRTLS problem into one of three canonical tractable formats, each then analyzed in detail.
result: The three transformed problem classes are characterized and thoroughly analyzed, yielding solution procedures for the singular-penalty case.
conclusion: Congruence-based simultaneous diagonalization provides an effective route to solving TRTLS with singular penalties, extending solvability beyond the nonsingular regime.

title: Unified Geometric--Kinematic Laws Of Mobility In 3d Cellular Networks
authors: Minghua Xia Tian Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23075v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mobility in three-dimensional (3D) cellular networks induces frequent handovers and random sojourn times for aerial users. Analyzing these events is challenging because they jointly depend on user trajectories and random service-boundary geometry. This paper develops a unified geometric--kinematic framework in which service regions form a stationary random tessellation, their boundaries constitute a random closed set, and user motion follows a cruise--turn mobility model. Under the stated stationarity, isotropy, and independence conditions, the handover rate satisfies the exact law \(H=(S_V/2)\bar v\), where \(S_V\) is the specific surface area and \(\bar v\) is the long-run mean speed. The forward boundary-distance distribution provides the local geometric input to an effective-traversal approximation for the mean remaining sojourn time. These results link global and local geometric descriptors to complementary mobility metrics. Combining the handover law with link coverage yields a handover-aware effective spectral efficiency for base station (BS) density selection and service-architecture comparison. We then specialize the framework to Poisson--Voronoi single-BS service and Poisson--Delaunay four-BS coordinated multi-point service; under both models, the handover rate scales as \(\lambda^{1/3}\bar v\). Numerical results corroborate the exact handover expressions, assess the sojourn-time approximations, and show how user speed and interruption duration affect the preferred density and architecture.
tldr: A stochastic-geometry framework deriving exact handover-rate and sojourn-time laws for mobile users in 3D cellular networks modeled by random tessellations.
motivation: Aerial users in 3D cellular networks experience frequent handovers and random sojourn times that depend jointly on trajectories and random service-boundary geometry, making analysis difficult.
method: Service regions are modeled as a stationary random tessellation with boundaries a random closed set, user motion follows a cruise-turn mobility model, and an effective-traversal approximation is used for mean remaining sojourn time; the framework is specialized to Poisson-Voronoi single-BS and Poisson-Delaunay four-BS coordinated multipoint service.
result: An exact handover law H = (S_V/2) v̄ is derived in terms of specific surface area and mean speed, and the handover rate is shown to scale as lambda^{1/3} v̄ under both service models, with numerical results corroborating the expressions.
conclusion: The work links global and local geometric descriptors to complementary mobility metrics and yields a handover-aware effective spectral efficiency for base-station density selection and architecture comparison.

title: Geometry-Aware Latent Representation Learning For Drag Coefficient Prediction Of Irregular Particles
authors: Zihao Li, Shota Deguchi, Mitsuteru Asai, Shunhua Chen, Naoto Mitsume
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting the drag coefficient [MATH] of irregular particles requires representing their complex three-dimensional geometry in a form suitable for predictive models. Empirical drag correlations and many data-driven models represent particle geometry through a small set of hand-crafted shape descriptors. Geometric differences omitted by these descriptors are unavailable to the predictor. We propose a variational autoencoder-multilayer perceptron (VAE-MLP) framework that learns a latent representation directly from voxelized particle geometry. Geometry reconstruction and drag coefficient prediction jointly guide the learning of this representation. We compare VAE-MLP with a descriptor-based MLP (Descriptor-MLP) and established empirical correlations using CFD data for synthetic particle geometries at Reynolds numbers of 10--200. When the evaluated geometric variations are represented in the training data, the two learned models achieve comparable accuracy for regular ellipsoids, while VAE-MLP yields lower errors for irregular particles. When high-order surface perturbations are excluded from training, VAE-MLP achieves lower overall mean absolute relative error in all five training runs. At the strongest tested perturbation, the mean errors across these runs are 4.97% for VAE-MLP and 9.88% for Descriptor-MLP. These results support learning geometric representations directly from particle geometry to improve drag prediction for the irregular geometries and unseen surface perturbations examined here.
tldr: A VAE-MLP framework learns latent representations directly from voxelized particle geometry to predict drag coefficients of irregular particles, outperforming hand-crafted shape descriptors.
motivation: Empirical drag correlations and descriptor-based data-driven models rely on a small set of hand-crafted shape descriptors, so geometric details omitted by those descriptors cannot inform the predictor.
method: A variational autoencoder encodes voxelized 3D particle geometry into a latent space, and a multilayer perceptron maps that latent code to drag coefficient; reconstruction and prediction losses jointly train the representation, benchmarked against a descriptor-based MLP and empirical correlations on CFD data at Re = 10–200.
result: For regular ellipsoids both learned models perform comparably, but VAE-MLP gives lower errors for irregular particles and unseen high-order surface perturbations, reaching 4.97% versus 9.88% mean absolute relative error at the strongest perturbation.
conclusion: Learning geometric representations directly from particle geometry improves drag prediction for irregular shapes and unseen perturbations, supporting geometry-aware latent representations over hand-crafted descriptors.

title: Stability And Error Estimates For Convolution Quadrature Under Radial Symbol Bounds
authors: Haibin Su Jingchuang Ren
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23163v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop stability and error estimates for multistep convolution quadrature (CQ) under general radial bounds on the Laplace symbol. Instead of the classical single-power condition [MATH], we assume [MATH] and consider two classes of radial functions: monotone bounds satisfying a scaling condition and regularly varying bounds with locally bounded above and away from zero. For strongly [MATH]-stable multistep methods, we derive approximation and stability estimates for the CQ weights, as well as error bounds for power-type inputs [MATH] with [MATH]. These estimates explicitly retain the dependence on the memory law through the factor [MATH]. The framework accommodates symbols whose behavior cannot be described by a global single-power. It also preserves slowly varying and multiscale factors that would be lost under a coarser power majorant. The theory is applied to fractional viscoelastic models, distributed-order operators, and logarithmic-power memory operators. Numerical experiments with backward Euler and second-order backward differentiation CQ confirm the expected temporal convergence orders for direct responses. Complementary evolution examples demonstrate the corresponding temporal behavior for smooth and nonsmooth initial data.
tldr: The paper develops stability and error estimates for multistep convolution quadrature methods under general radial bounds on the Laplace symbol, extending beyond the classical single-power condition.
motivation: Classical convolution quadrature theory assumes a single-power bound on the Laplace symbol, which fails to capture slowly varying, multiscale, or logarithmic memory kernels arising in fractional and distributed-order models.
method: The authors assume radial symbol bounds and treat two function classes—monotone bounds with a scaling condition and regularly varying bounds locally bounded above and away from zero—deriving approximation and stability estimates for CQ weights and error bounds for power-type inputs.
result: They obtain estimates that explicitly retain dependence on the memory law through a multiplicative factor, and confirm the predicted temporal convergence orders numerically for backward Euler and second-order BDF convolution quadrature.
conclusion: The framework handles symbols not describable by a global single power and preserves slowly varying and multiscale factors, with applications to fractional viscoelastic models, distributed-order operators, and logarithmic-power memory operators.

title: Multilevel Gaussian Processes With Applications To Inverse Problems
authors: Stjepan Salatovic, Aretha L. Teckentrup, Sebastian Krumscheid
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a multilevel Gaussian process (GP) regression framework for approximating functions that are accessible only through a hierarchy of approximations of increasing accuracy and computational cost. One example is the response surface of a parametrized partial differential equation, where the hierarchy arises from the resolution of the numerical solver. Modeling level increments independently with Mat\'ern-kernel GPs and allocating samples flexibly across discretization levels yields substantial computational savings over single-level GP regression. We derive [MATH] convergence rates for the posterior mean and variance, accounting for maximum likelihood estimation of the marginal variance and for kernel misspecification. When increment regularity or solver cost is unknown a priori, an adaptive sequential-design algorithm with cost-adapted active learning criteria allocates samples across levels. We apply the surrogate to Bayesian inverse problems, for which Hellinger distance bounds between the true and approximate posteriors are known. Numerical experiments illustrate the theoretical rates and the resulting computational savings.
tldr: The paper develops a multilevel Gaussian process regression framework that exploits hierarchies of increasingly accurate and costly approximations to build cheap surrogates for expensive function evaluations.
motivation: Many scientific computations, such as parametrized PDE solvers, only provide function values through a hierarchy of discretizations, and single-level GP regression wastes budget by ignoring inexpensive low-fidelity evaluations.
method: Level increments are modeled independently with Matern-kernel GPs, samples are allocated flexibly across levels, and convergence rates for posterior mean and variance are derived accounting for maximum-likelihood estimation and kernel misspecification, plus an adaptive sequential design with cost-adapted active learning.
result: Theoretical convergence rates are established and validated numerically, showing substantial computational savings over single-level GP regression, and the surrogate is applied to Bayesian inverse problems with Hellinger distance bounds between true and approximate posteriors.
conclusion: Multilevel GP surrogates provide an efficient, theoretically grounded tool for uncertainty quantification and Bayesian inversion of expensive hierarchical models.

title: Orthogonal Projections And Assouad Dimension: Resolving Fraser's Questions
authors: Bilel Selmi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.23295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine two questions on exceptional orthogonal projections for Assouad dimension. Let [MATH]. The planar packing question, Question 17.8.2, is already answered affirmatively by Wu's countability theorem. Using that theorem, we also describe the distinction between planar sets of Assouad dimension at most [MATH] and those of dimension greater than [MATH] when they are embedded in higher-dimensional spaces. The computations use elementary Grassmannian geometry; we make no claim of a new planar projection theorem or of an optimal bound for arbitrary higher-dimensional sets.
tldr: A pure geometric measure theory paper resolving Fraser's questions on exceptional orthogonal projections and Assouad dimension of planar and higher-dimensional sets.
motivation: Questions about how Assouad dimension behaves under generic orthogonal projections remained partly open for planar sets and for low-dimensional sets embedded in higher-dimensional spaces.
method: The author applies Wu's countability theorem together with elementary Grassmannian geometry to characterize the projection behavior and distinguish sets of Assouad dimension at most one from those of larger dimension.
result: The planar packing question (Question 17.8.2) is confirmed to admit an affirmative answer via Wu's theorem, and a description of exceptional projection sets for higher-dimensional embeddings is obtained.
conclusion: The work clarifies projection phenomena for Assouad dimension but explicitly claims no new planar projection theorem nor an optimal bound for arbitrary higher-dimensional sets.

title: Everyone's A Little Bit Racist: A Novel Ml Backdoor Attack In Black-box Mode
authors: Gabriele Costa Michele Cerrta
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22459v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Backdoors are among the most impactful attacks against Machine Learning (ML), yet most existing methods assume some form of training-time poisoning or direct model manipulation. This is often considered sufficient to assume that existing systems are not exposed to actual risks. In this paper, we introduce Backdoor-as-a-Service, a model-agnostic, fully black-box technique that, instead of installing a backdoor, activates it in the form of a latent secondary task leveraging on an already present behavior. Our tool uses genetic search to discover input transformations that induce systematic output differences aligned with an attacker-defined task, without modifying training data, architecture, or weights. We verify our approach against two targets. First, we target a MNIST digits classifier that we coerce into implementing a binary letter-recognition task. Then, we attack a production-grade NSFW classifier using face-specific perturbations to turn it into a proxy for demographic-group classification. In both cases, our method successfully enables the target backdoor. Finally, we discuss the existing countermeasures to assess the actual risk for the deployed systems.
tldr: The paper presents 'Backdoor-as-a-Service', a black-box, model-agnostic method that activates latent behaviors in existing ML classifiers as attacker-defined secondary tasks rather than implanting new backdoors.
motivation: Most backdoor attacks assume training-time poisoning or direct weight access, leading practitioners to believe deployed systems are safe; the authors show this assumption is false.
method: A genetic search discovers input transformations that induce systematic, task-aligned output differences without modifying training data, architecture, or weights, evaluated on an MNIST digit classifier coerced into letter recognition and a production NSFW classifier repurposed for demographic-group classification.
result: Both attacks succeed in activating the target backdoor behaviors, and the authors survey existing countermeasures to assess the residual risk for deployed systems.
conclusion: Latent secondary tasks can be exploited as backdoors in fully black-box settings, so deployment-time threat models must extend beyond training-time poisoning.

title: StratFL: Countering Covert Model Poisoning Attacks With Strategic Federated Learning
authors: Venkata Sriram Siddhardh Nadendla Manoj Twarakavi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advanced persistent threats (APTs) are a major concern in federated learning (FL) deployments in critical sectors such as healthcare, and finance. Traditional defense mechanisms fail to contain APTs due to their intermittent attacking behavior. This paper addresses a specific type of APT called covert model poisoning (CMP) where the attacker intermittently injects poisoned model updates in a covert manner. The interaction between the FL server and a CMP attacker is modeled as an imperfect repeated game where both players cannot observe each other's actions. A novel adversarial search algorithm called StratFL is designed alongside novel belief update algorithms at both the server and adversary. Experiments are designed using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets to evaluate and compare StratFL's performance against state-of-the-art methods. Empirical convergence of belief update algorithms is demonstrated across various security vignettes. At the same time, StratFL is found to exhibit an improved accuracy of 10% compared to state-of-the-art methods.
tldr: StratFL is an adversarial search algorithm with belief-update mechanisms that defends federated learning servers against intermittently injected covert model poisoning attacks modeled as an imperfect repeated game.
motivation: Advanced persistent threats in federated learning, particularly covert model poisoning where attackers inject poisoned updates intermittently, evade traditional defenses and threaten critical sectors such as healthcare and finance.
method: The server-attacker interaction is cast as an imperfect repeated game with unobserved actions, and a novel adversarial search algorithm (StratFL) is designed together with belief-update algorithms for both the server and the adversary.
result: Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 show empirical convergence of the belief-update algorithms across security vignettes, and StratFL achieves about 10% higher accuracy than state-of-the-art defenses.
conclusion: Strategic, game-theoretic defense with belief updating can effectively counter intermittent covert poisoning in federated learning, improving robustness and model accuracy.

title: Ace: An AI-Orchestrated Intrusion Detection And Compliance Mapping Engine
authors: Abdoulie Ceesay, Rishikesh Sahay, Md Rasel Al Mamun, Bell Raj Eapen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study proposes the Automated Compliance Engine (ACE), an AI-orchestrated framework that links intrusion detection, regulatory control mapping, and automated countermeasure deployment for security operations environments. ACE integrates Suricata IDS, a LangGraph five-stage workflow, retrieval-augmented generation, NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control retrieval, large language model-based control ranking, and SSH-based Suricata rule deployment. The framework was evaluated in a two-virtual-machine laboratory using eight simulated attack scenarios and three legitimate traffic tests. ACE processed all eight attack alerts, achieved 100% alert detection, 0% false positives across legitimate traffic tests, generated deployable AUTO rules for 37.5% of alerts, verified 100% deployment of generated rules, and achieved an average NIST control-mapping confidence score of 0.87. The DeepEval assessment produced 1.0 scores for answer relevancy and faithfulness, while the hallucination score reflected known LLM-as-judge calibration limitations. The evaluation was conducted in a controlled environment with a limited attack set. Further validation is required using enterprise-scale telemetry, multiple IDS sensors, and an analyst-in-the-loop review. The results demonstrate how AI-assisted security automation can reduce analyst effort in translating IDS alerts into compliance-relevant evidence and defensive actions. ACE contributes an integrated detection-to-compliance-to-response workflow combining IDS telemetry, RAG-based control mapping, and automated rule deployment.
tldr: ACE is an AI-orchestrated security framework that chains Suricata intrusion detection, retrieval-augmented NIST SP 800-53 control mapping, LLM-based control ranking, and automated SSH deployment of IDS rules.
motivation: Security operations teams struggle to translate raw IDS alerts into compliance-relevant evidence and concrete defensive actions, which consumes substantial analyst effort.
method: A LangGraph five-stage workflow orchestrates Suricata telemetry ingestion, RAG-based retrieval of NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 controls, LLM ranking of candidate controls, rule generation, and SSH-based deployment, evaluated on two VMs with eight simulated attacks and three legitimate-traffic tests.
result: The system detected 100% of attack alerts with zero false positives on legitimate traffic, produced deployable rules for 37.5% of alerts with 100% deployment success, and achieved an average control-mapping confidence of 0.87 and DeepEval scores of 1.0 for answer relevancy and faithfulness.
conclusion: The authors present an integrated detection-to-compliance-to-response pipeline that reduces analyst effort, while acknowledging that validation was limited to a controlled lab setting and requires enterprise-scale telemetry and analyst-in-the-loop review.

title: Optimally Curating An Event
authors: Mohammadtaghi Hajiaghayi, Sebastien Lahaie, Mohammad Mahdavi, Suho Shin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the optimal design of a self-financing event, a problem that requires balancing the recruitment of costly, positive-value participants with revenue-generating agents who may impose negative values on the event. We introduce a novel two-sided mechanism design framework with plus agents equipped with private costs and positive impact, and minus agents with private values and negative impact upon inclusion in the event, to maximize the overall quality of the event under a budget-balanced (BB) constraint so that the designer does not run a deficit. We conduct a comprehensive study on the theory of optimal event curation on various utility functions. For additive utility, we fully characterize the optimal incentive-compatible Bayesian mechanism under both the ex-ante and ex-post BB constraints. For submodular utility, we propose an ex-ante BB mechanism that achieves a constant-factor approximation to the optimal Bayesian mechanism.
tldr: The paper studies optimal self-financing event curation via a two-sided Bayesian mechanism design framework balancing paid positive-value participants ('plus agents') against revenue-generating but harmful 'minus agents' under budget balance.
motivation: Designers of events must recruit costly contributors while admitting revenue-generating participants who may degrade event quality, so a principled mechanism is needed that avoids running a deficit.
method: The authors formulate a two-sided mechanism design problem with plus agents holding private costs and minus agents holding private values, and derive optimal incentive-compatible Bayesian mechanisms for additive utility under ex-ante and ex-post budget balance, plus a constant-factor approximation for submodular utility.
result: For additive utilities the optimal IC Bayesian mechanism is fully characterized under both ex-ante and ex-post budget balance, while for submodular utilities an ex-ante budget-balanced mechanism attains a constant-factor approximation to the optimal Bayesian mechanism.
conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for event curation as a budget-balanced two-sided mechanism design problem and extends tractable guarantees to non-additive (submodular) valuations.

title: Veil-Then-Reveal: Protecting Pii Privacy Via Reversible Pseudo-Anonymization In Zero-Trust User--LLM Interaction
authors: Mohamed Shaaban, Mohamed Elmahallawy, Thomas E. Carroll
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly process sensitive documents and personal information, yet sending prompts containing personally identifiable information (PII) to remote providers exposes data subjects and organizations to risks from logging, retention, model training, and unintended disclosure. Existing anonymization methods often mask or remove PII, while conventional encryption eliminates the lexical and structural cues needed for effective LLM processing. We present Veil-then-Reveal (VtR), a user-side PII pseudo-anonymization framework for privacy-preserving LLM interaction under a zero-trust threat model. VtR treats remote LLM providers as untrusted and sends only pseudo-anonymized prompts, keeping plaintext PII on the user. VtR first detects PII and replaces it with realistic, same-type, in-vocabulary surrogates before prompts leave the user's device, preserving their linguistic and structural properties. It combines format-preserving encryption (FPE) for structured PII, such as phone and credit-card numbers, with a keyed-hash dictionary and secure vault for semantic PII, such as names, locations, and organizations. Session-specific mappings provide cross-session unlinkability, while user-side restoration reversibly replaces surrogates with their original values in LLM responses. We further introduce a rank-class FPE strategy for dates that preserves format and ambiguity while reducing cipher evaluations. Evaluation on three datasets containing 11,322 annotated PII instances achieves 97.9% detection recall, 95.2% protection of detected values, and 99.9% round trip; 100% of echoed surrogates end-to-end round-trip restoration.
tldr: VtR is a user-side pseudo-anonymization framework that replaces PII with realistic same-type surrogates before prompts reach an untrusted LLM provider, then reversibly restores the originals in responses.
motivation: Sending prompts containing personally identifiable information to remote LLM providers exposes users and organizations to logging, retention, training, and disclosure risks, while masking or encryption destroys the lexical and structural cues LLMs need.
method: The framework detects PII and substitutes in-vocabulary surrogates, combining format-preserving encryption for structured PII (phone, credit-card numbers) with a keyed-hash dictionary and secure vault for semantic PII, plus a rank-class FPE scheme for dates and session-specific mappings for unlinkability.
result: Evaluation on three datasets with 11,322 annotated PII instances yields 97.9% detection recall, 95.2% protection of detected values, 99.9% round-trip recovery, and full end-to-end restoration of echoed surrogates.
conclusion: The work offers a practical privacy layer for zero-trust human-LLM interaction, though it lies entirely outside quantum information science and is only tangentially connected through generic cryptographic primitives.

title: Grad: Graph-Structured Antibody Defense For Llm Agents
authors: Tianqi Song, Jiawei Du, Xuemei Jia, Zheng Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory poisoning and decomposition attacks distribute malicious evidence across the operations of large language model agents. Existing request-level defenses can miss such attacks because they assess individual inputs without connecting earlier information to later actions. Moreover, detectors must adapt as task contexts change, while updates to shared parameters can impair previously learned detection capabilities. To address these challenges, we propose GRAD, which combines graph-based evidence aggregation across operations with an extensible collection of detection experts. Its Semantic-Structural Understanding Module (SSUM) jointly encodes operation text, event attributes, and typed candidate relations in an execution graph to aggregate distributed attack evidence into a graph-level risk score. Its Continual Antibody Adaptation (CAA) adds experts on frozen encoder snapshots and routes inputs by observable graph signatures, acquiring and reusing detection capabilities as tasks arrive. Across Decomp, MCP, and MRT, GRAD achieves AUROCs of 97.19%, 77.59%, and 86.60%, respectively, outperforming Sequential Monitor and locally adapted Agent-Sentry and NeuroTaint. CAA improves final accuracy by 13.08 percentage points over Replay on the cross-dataset task stream. The gain remains 9.05 points with equal family/base-case weights within each task. Its compact drop-in gate performs local model inference in milliseconds without monitoring API calls.
tldr: GRAD is a graph-structured defense framework that aggregates distributed malicious evidence across an LLM agent's execution trace to detect memory-poisoning and decomposition attacks.
motivation: Request-level detectors miss attacks that spread malicious evidence across multiple operations, and shared-parameter fine-tuning for new tasks causes catastrophic forgetting of previously learned detection capabilities.
method: The Semantic-Structural Understanding Module encodes operation text, event attributes, and typed relations into an execution graph producing a graph-level risk score, while Continual Antibody Adaptation adds experts on frozen encoder snapshots and routes inputs by observable graph signatures.
result: GRAD reaches AUROCs of 97.19%, 77.59%, and 86.60% on Decomp, MCP, and MRT, beating Sequential Monitor and adapted Agent-Sentry/NeuroTaint, with CAA improving cross-dataset accuracy by 13.08 points over Replay (9.05 with balanced weights).
conclusion: Graph-level evidence aggregation plus modular continual expert addition yields a compact millisecond-latency gate that hardens LLM agents against distributed poisoning without extra API monitoring calls.

title: The Source Of Data Value: Consumer Disclosure, Access Design, And Platform Monetization
authors: Hexiao Liu, Lijian Lu, Mingzheng Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22864v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital marketplaces increasingly earn revenue from transaction commissions and seller-facing data services. Sellers may purchase data to increase revenue or avoid competing with an informed rival. We examine how consumer disclosure rights shape these motives and the platform's incentive to provide data. We develop a game-theoretic model of a commissioned platform, two differentiated sellers, and privacy-sensitive consumers. Data generates value through bilateral sales-revenue gains and competition threats arising from asymmetric access. Under mandatory collection, the platform can monetize defensive adoption, even when bilateral personalization reduces seller revenue. Under voluntary disclosure, anonymous purchasing and strictly positive privacy costs make unilateral disclosure unattractive in the baseline. Exclusive access thus yields no usable information, restores sellers' no-data rejection payoffs, and eliminates defensive fees. Profitable provision therefore requires nonnegative bilateral revenue gains. Under full fee extraction, sellers retain their no-data net profits. This revenue alignment does not guarantee welfare gains: additional transactions may benefit consumers, whereas segmentation in an already covered market can raise anonymous prices and reduce welfare. Capping anonymous offers at their no-data benchmark protects individual consumers and limits positive-mass provision to the transaction-creation region. Extensions consider access choice, heterogeneous privacy costs, imperfect identification, and limited contractual credibility. Platforms should evaluate data services based on both bilateral-use and seller-rejection outcomes, and sellers should distinguish revenue-enhancing from defensive investments. Regulators should distinguish equal-access rules from effective consumer control and monitor pricing in anonymous channels.
tldr: A game-theoretic analysis of how consumer data-disclosure rights and platform access design shape a commissioned marketplace's incentives to sell seller-facing data services.
motivation: Digital platforms increasingly monetize data sold to sellers, and policymakers debate consumer disclosure rights; the authors ask how disclosure rules and access exclusivity alter seller data-purchase motives (revenue enhancement vs. defensive adoption) and welfare.
method: A stylized game-theoretic model with a commissioned platform, two differentiated sellers, and privacy-sensitive consumers, analyzed under mandatory collection versus voluntary disclosure, with extensions for access choice, heterogeneous privacy costs, imperfect identification, and limited contractual credibility.
result: Under mandatory collection platforms can monetize defensive adoption; under voluntary disclosure exclusive access yields no usable information and eliminates defensive fees, so profitable provision requires nonnegative bilateral revenue gains, and fee extraction leaves sellers at no-data profits while segmentation can raise anonymous prices and reduce welfare.
conclusion: Platforms should judge data services by both bilateral-use and seller-rejection outcomes, and regulators should distinguish equal-access rules from effective consumer control while monitoring anonymous-channel pricing.

title: Stealthy Poisoning Attacks Via Reused Kv Cache Of Reasoning
authors: L. Zhu, Y. Jung, S. Szyller
abstract: ArXiv:2610.22873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern large language model (LLM) systems reuse key-value (KV) caches to accelerate inference. Recent work has shown that reusing KV caches from reasoning traces can also improve task performance, similar to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We demonstrate that this form of KV cache reuse introduces new poisoning vulnerabilities. We propose R[MATH]ECAP (Reused Reasoning-Cache Poisoning), a black-box attack that plants poisoned reasoning traces solely through interactions with a system's chat interface. R[MATH]ECAP constructs two traces: a preceding trace that steers the model toward an adversarial target and a retained trace that carries this target.
